# Distributed transactions {#sec-distributed-transactions}

A transaction in one database is atomic; a change that spans two databases, or two services, is not, unless something makes it so. Liu puts the
problem in one sentence: "A distributed transaction is a transaction that involves more than one data source where the complexity comes when a
subset of the data sources successfully commits. At the same time, the other subset fails to commit" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Distributed Transaction"]. This chapter defines the ways of making such changes all-or-nothing, or of making their partial states harmless: atomic
commitment, globally meaningful timestamps, sagas, the transactional outbox, and the checks that keep concurrent requests from colliding across
services.

The claims are of two kinds. Atomic commitment, physical clocks and TrueTime, sagas, the outbox and cross-service concurrency control are
definitions. Five results with complete proofs make them precise: what two-phase commit guarantees and why it blocks, why commit wait gives external
consistency, what a saga's compensations restore, what an outbox relay publishes, and what conditional writes, unique slots and holds prevent.
Lamport's theorem on synchronising physical clocks is quoted, with its source. The transactions and isolation of @def-transaction-isolation, the
consensus of @def-consensus and the outbox of @def-event-sourcing are used by link.

The sources are the benchmark books, @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Ch. 5, Ch. 15 and App. D], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5],
@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Chs. 4 and 8], @gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Ch. 10] and @pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024
[Ch. 10], with two papers: @corbett2012spanner on Spanner and TrueTime, and @lamport1978time on physical clocks. The original paper on sagas
(Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) was not available; sagas are taken from the books, which cite it.

The chapter has five sections. @sec-atomic-commit defines atomic commitment and two-phase commit and proves its safety and its blocking.
@sec-spanner defines physical clocks, TrueTime and external consistency and proves that commit wait yields it. @sec-sagas defines sagas and
proves what compensation restores. @sec-outbox defines the outbox relay and reconciliation and proves what the relay publishes.
@sec-cross-service defines locks, optimistic checks and reservations across services and proves what each prevents.

The running example is the photo service of the earlier chapters: an upload writes a photo to the blob store and a row to the metadata database
(Liu's own example), and a new feature sells prints of photos, which charges a card, books a slot at a print shop and arranges shipping.

Every definition and theorem is followed by ten examples and ten exercises, each exercise with a hidden solution in two tabs: the argument, then a
computation with its recorded output. The computations run in plain Python 3.12 with NumPy and the standard library's `sqlite3`; protocols are
simulated with seeded random failures. Diagrams are written in the D2 language. Code for particular workflow engines is shown as illustrative code
and is not run.

## Atomic commitment and two-phase commit {#sec-atomic-commit}

When a change spans several data stores, each can commit its part or not, and atomicity means that they all do the same. Liu: "Usually, a system can
write to multiple sources with 2-phase commit (2PC) with a prepare and a commit phase. The idea for 2PC is that once both sources decide they are ok
with the commit, the coordinator will continue to push the 2nd phase commit until they go through" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5,
"Distributed Transaction"]. This section defines atomic commitment and two-phase commit, and proves that two-phase commit is safe and that it can
block.

For more on this topic, see @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [App. D, pp. 418-421], @liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Distributed Transaction"]
and @corbett2012spanner [Sec. 4.2.1].

### Participants, votes and decisions

A coordinator asks every participant whether it can commit, and decides only once all have answered. @fig-ac-2pc shows a successful run.

![Two-phase commit between a coordinator and two participants. The participants prepare and vote; the coordinator logs the decision and then sends
it.](figures/twopc_sequence.svg){#fig-ac-2pc width=75%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-atomic-commit}
#### Atomic commitment and two-phase commit

1. A **distributed transaction** changes data at several **participants**, databases or services, each of which can commit or abort its own part.
   An **atomic commitment protocol** lets each participant **vote** yes or no and then **decide** commit or abort, at most once, so that:
   (**agreement**) no two participants decide differently; (**validity**) commit is decided only if every participant voted yes; (**non-triviality**)
   if every participant votes yes and nothing fails, commit is decided.
2. In **two-phase commit** (2PC) a **coordinator** sends a prepare request to every participant. A participant that can commit makes its part durable
   without making it visible, logs that it is **prepared** and votes yes; otherwise it votes no and aborts. If all vote yes the coordinator logs
   commit and sends commit to all; if any votes no or does not answer, it logs abort and sends abort. Participants apply the decision and acknowledge.
3. A participant that has voted yes and not yet learnt the decision is **in doubt**: it may neither commit nor abort on its own, and keeps the locks
   of its part. A protocol is **blocking** if a failure can leave a participant in doubt for as long as the failure lasts.
:::

::::

Item 2 follows Tan: "The coordinator first sends a prepare request to every database ... If every database responds successfully, the coordinator then
sends a commit request to every database. If any database does not respond or responds with an error, the coordinator sends an abort request to every
database" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, p. 418]. Item 3 is Tan's remedy for inconsistency, "participating databases neither committing nor
aborting transactions until their outcome is explicitly decided", which "has the downside that those transactions may hold locks and block other
transactions for a long time until the coordinator comes back" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, p. 420]. The three properties of item 1 are the
usual statement of the problem; none of the sources read lists them.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Liu's first example is a money transfer across two databases. Without atomic commitment one write can succeed alone.

::: {#exm-ac-liu-transfer}
#### A transfer between two databases

Liu's code adds the amount to the receiver's database and then removes it from the sender's: "This call is problematic when add_amount is
committed successfully and remove_amount fails to commit. Perhaps the from user no longer has enough balance, or the from_user_database is just
unavailable now" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Distributed Transaction"]. The money is created: item 1's agreement fails.

```{.python .run}
balances = {"alice": 50, "bob": 0}
def send_money(frm, to, amount, sender_db_up):
    balances[to] += amount                       # committed in the receiver's database
    if not sender_db_up: return "remove failed"
    balances[frm] -= amount
print(send_money("alice", "bob", 30, sender_db_up=False), balances, "total", sum(balances.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
remove failed {'alice': 50, 'bob': 30} total 80
```
:::

The photo service's upload writes two stores. Liu orders the writes so that a failure leaves only harmless garbage.

::: {#exm-ac-photo-upload}
#### A photo and its row

Persisting the metadata first and then the photo can leave "a metadata row with no photo blob"; persisting the blob first, then the row with its
URL, leaves at worst "an unreferenced blob", which "a background cleanup job" can clear [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Blob Storage and
Metadata Storage"]. No atomic commitment is used: the order makes the partial state invisible to readers.
:::

A run of item 2 with two participants. The coordinator decides only after both votes.

::: {#exm-ac-run}
#### Two-phase commit in code

Both participants can commit, so both vote yes and the coordinator decides commit.

```{.python .run}
class Participant:
    def __init__(self, name, can_commit): self.name, self.can, self.log = name, can_commit, []
    def prepare(self):
        self.log.append("prepared" if self.can else "aborted"); return self.can
    def decide(self, d): self.log.append(d)
parts = [Participant("photos", True), Participant("billing", True)]
coord_log = []
votes = [p.prepare() for p in parts]
decision = "commit" if all(votes) else "abort"
coord_log.append(decision)                      # logged before it is sent
for p in parts: p.decide(decision)
print(coord_log, [(p.name, p.log) for p in parts])
```

```{.text .run-output}
['commit'] [('photos', ['prepared', 'commit']), ('billing', ['prepared', 'commit'])]
```
:::

Validity in a run. A single no vote aborts everything.

::: {#exm-ac-no-vote}
#### One participant refuses

The billing participant cannot commit, votes no and aborts at once; the coordinator decides abort and the photos participant, which had prepared,
discards its prepared part.

```{.python .run}
votes = {"photos": True, "billing": False}
decision = "commit" if all(votes.values()) else "abort"
print("decision:", decision, "| photos keeps its change:", decision == "commit")
```

```{.text .run-output}
decision: abort | photos keeps its change: False
```
:::

Tan shows a coordinator crash leaving databases inconsistent. Item 3 is what prevents it.

::: {#exm-ac-tan-crash}
#### A crash during the second phase

Tan's figure shows that "a coordinator crash during the commit phase may cause inconsistency, as certain databases will commit, but the rest will
abort" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, p. 419]. That happens only if an in-doubt participant decides on its own, for example by timing out to
abort; under item 3 it waits instead, and the cost is blocking.
:::

Every participant must speak the coordinator's protocol. Tan names the standard.

::: {#exm-ac-xa}
#### A standard interface

"2PC requires all databases to implement a common API to interact with the coordinator. The standard is called X/Open XA (eXtended Architecture)";
and "many modern technologies do not support 2PC. Examples include NoSQL databases, like Cassandra and MongoDB, and message brokers, like Kafka and
RabbitMQ" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, pp. 420-421].
:::

Tan lists the reasons against 2PC between services. Most are about availability and ownership.

::: {#exm-ac-tan-services}
#### Why services avoid it

Among them: "All databases must respond for a commit to occur ... There is no graceful degradation"; the cost of "development and maintenance of 2PC
in every service/database involved"; and "2PC reduces availability, as all participating services must be available for commits"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, pp. 420-421]. With participants of availability $0.999$, a five-participant commit succeeds only when all five
are up, $0.995$ of the time.

```{.python .run}
print(f"{0.999 ** 5:.4f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
0.9950
```
:::

Gilbert gives scaling as the reason distributed transactions are avoided. Spanner's measurements give a more nuanced picture.

::: {#exm-ac-gilbert}
#### Fallen out of favour

"Distributed transactions have fallen out of favor because the two-phase commit cycle does not scale" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024,
Ch. 4, "Stream-first event sourcing"]. Spanner reports that "two-phase commit can scale to a reasonable number of participants ... Scaling up to 50
participants is reasonable in both mean and 99th-percentile, and latencies start to rise noticeably at 100 participants" [@corbett2012spanner,
Sec. 5.1].
:::

Spanner's Table 4 gives the mean latency of a two-phase commit. It grows slowly up to fifty participants.

::: {#exm-ac-spanner-table}
#### Latency against participants

The means are $17.0$, $24.5$, $31.5$, $30.0$, $35.5$, $42.7$, $71.4$ and $150.5\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $1$, $2$, $5$, $10$, $25$, $50$, $100$ and $200$
participants [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 5.1, Table 4]; from $50$ to $200$ the latency more than triples.

```{.python .run}
n = [1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200]
mean = [17.0, 24.5, 31.5, 30.0, 35.5, 42.7, 71.4, 150.5]
for a, b in zip(n, mean): print(f"{a:3d} participants: {b:6.1f} ms")
print(f"200 vs 50: x{mean[-1] / mean[5]:.1f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
  1 participants:   17.0 ms
  2 participants:   24.5 ms
  5 participants:   31.5 ms
 10 participants:   30.0 ms
 25 participants:   35.5 ms
 50 participants:   42.7 ms
100 participants:   71.4 ms
200 participants:  150.5 ms
200 vs 50: x3.5
```
:::

A prepared participant keeps its locks. Item 3's cost is other transactions waiting.

::: {#exm-ac-locks}
#### Locks held while in doubt

A prepared photo row is locked until the decision arrives; a coordinator that is down for $10$ minutes keeps it locked for $10$ minutes, and every
request that needs the row waits or fails. With $50$ requests a second for the row, $3 \times 10^4$ requests are affected.

```{.python .run}
print("affected requests:", 50 * 600)
```

```{.text .run-output}
affected requests: 30000
```
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise compares Liu's two orders for the upload. One leaves a dangling reference, the other an orphan.

::: {#exr-ac-order}
#### Which write first

For an upload that writes a blob and a metadata row without atomic commitment, list what a failure between the writes leaves in each order, and
which state a reader can see.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Row first: a row pointing to a missing blob, which a reader sees as a broken photo. Blob first: an unreferenced blob, which no reader can reach,
and which a cleanup job removes. The second order keeps every visible state consistent.

## Python

Both orders with a failure in between.

```{.python .run}
def upload(order):
    blobs, rows = set(), {}
    first = order[0]
    if first == "row": rows["p1"] = "blob-p1"
    else: blobs.add("blob-p1")
    # failure: the second write never happens
    broken = [r for r, b in rows.items() if b not in blobs]
    orphans = [b for b in blobs if b not in rows.values()]
    return {"broken rows": broken, "orphan blobs": orphans}
print("row first:", upload(["row", "blob"]), "| blob first:", upload(["blob", "row"]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
row first: {'broken rows': ['p1'], 'orphan blobs': []} | blob first: {'broken rows': [], 'orphan blobs': ['blob-p1']}
```
::::
:::

The second exercise removes the prepare phase. Liu states the consequence.

::: {#exr-ac-one-phase}
#### Why one phase is not enough

Show with two participants that a coordinator that sends "commit" directly, without asking, can violate agreement, as Liu notes: "If there's only 1
phase, if one commits and the other one decides it can't commit, the system will be in an inconsistent state" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020,
Ch. 5, "Distributed Transaction"].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The first participant commits on receipt; the second finds a constraint violated and aborts. They decided differently. The prepare phase moves
every reason to refuse before any commit: a participant that votes yes has already ensured it can commit.

## Python

Both protocols.

```{.python .run}
can = {"A": True, "B": False}
one_phase = {p: ("commit" if ok else "abort") for p, ok in can.items()}
d = "commit" if all(can.values()) else "abort"
two_phase = {p: d for p in can}
print("one phase:", one_phase, "| two phase:", two_phase)
```

```{.text .run-output}
one phase: {'A': 'commit', 'B': 'abort'} | two phase: {'A': 'abort', 'B': 'abort'}
```
::::
:::

The third exercise lets a participant time out. Before voting it may abort; after voting it may not.

::: {#exr-ac-timeout-abort}
#### A timeout before voting

A participant has not yet received the prepare request after $30\,\mathrm{s}$ and aborts its part. Is agreement at risk? What if it had already voted
yes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Before voting it is safe: it will vote no, or not at all, and the coordinator, missing its yes, can only decide abort. After voting yes it is in doubt
(item 3): the coordinator may have decided commit from its vote, so aborting could disagree with participants that committed.

## Python

The coordinator's rule against both timings.

```{.python .run}
def coordinator(votes): return "commit" if votes and all(votes) else "abort"
print("timed out before voting:", coordinator([True, False]))
print("others commit on a yes it sent, so a later local abort disagrees:", coordinator([True, True]), "vs abort")
```

```{.text .run-output}
timed out before voting: abort
others commit on a yes it sent, so a later local abort disagrees: commit vs abort
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise prices Tan's objection. Every participant must be up for a commit.

::: {#exr-ac-availability}
#### Availability of a commit

Participants are up independently with probability $0.999$. Find the probability that a commit can proceed with $2$, $5$ and $20$ participants, and the
expected number of failed commits a day at $100$ transactions per second with $5$ participants.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$0.999^n$: $0.998$, $0.995$ and $0.980$ (@prp-series-parallel-availability). At $8.64 \times 10^6$ transactions a day and $0.5\%$ failures,
$4.3 \times 10^4$ fail.

## Python

The products.

```{.python .run}
for n in (2, 5, 20): print(n, f"{0.999 ** n:.4f}")
print(f"failed per day with 5: {100 * 86400 * (1 - 0.999 ** 5):.3g}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
2 0.9980
5 0.9950
20 0.9802
failed per day with 5: 4.31e+04
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise measures item 3's window in a normal run. It is one round trip plus a log write.

::: {#exr-ac-in-doubt-time}
#### How long a participant is in doubt

Round trips between coordinator and participants take $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ and a forced log write $1\,\mathrm{ms}$. From the moment a participant votes, how
long is it in doubt in a run without failures?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Its vote reaches the coordinator after half a round trip, the coordinator logs the decision ($1\,\mathrm{ms}$, once the last vote is in) and the decision
travels back in half a round trip: $1 + 1 + 1 = 3\,\mathrm{ms}$ for the slowest voter, longer for one that voted early.

## Python

The sum.

```{.python .run}
rtt, log = 2.0, 1.0
print("in doubt:", rtt / 2 + log + rtt / 2, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
in doubt: 3.0 ms
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise restarts the coordinator. Its log tells it what to resend.

::: {#exr-ac-recovery}
#### A coordinator that recovers

The coordinator crashes after logging commit and sending it to one of two participants. On recovery, what must it do, and what if it crashed before
logging any decision?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With commit logged, it resends commit to every participant that has not acknowledged; the decision cannot change. With nothing logged, no participant
can have received a decision, so it may decide abort and send it; Tan's point that "the coordinator must log all transactions, so during a crash recovery it
can compare its log to the databases" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, p. 420].

## Python

Recovery from the log.

```{.python .run}
def recover(log, acked, participants):
    decision = log[-1] if log else "abort"
    return decision, [p for p in participants if p not in acked]
print(recover(["commit"], {"A"}, ["A", "B"]), recover([], set(), ["A", "B"]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
('commit', ['B']) ('abort', ['A', 'B'])
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise merges the coordinator with one participant. It saves a round trip for that participant.

::: {#exr-ac-coordinator-vote}
#### The coordinator as a participant

In Spanner the coordinator is itself a participant: "The coordinator leader also first acquires write locks, but skips the prepare phase"
[@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.1]. Why may it skip the prepare phase?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The prepare phase lets a participant promise to commit before the decision. The coordinator makes the decision itself, so it never needs to promise:
it holds its locks, and its own decision record also records its part. The other participants still prepare.

## Python

Messages with and without a separate coordinator, for $n$ participants.

```{.python .run}
for n in (2, 5):
    print(n, "participants: separate coordinator", 4 * n, "messages; coordinator is a participant", 4 * (n - 1))
```

```{.text .run-output}
2 participants: separate coordinator 8 messages; coordinator is a participant 4
5 participants: separate coordinator 20 messages; coordinator is a participant 16
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise checks Tan's figure against item 3. Inconsistency needs a participant to break the rules.

::: {#exr-ac-tan-inconsistency}
#### Is two-phase commit inconsistent?

Tan writes that "a weakness of 2PC is that the coordinator must be available throughout the process, or inconsistency may result"
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, p. 419]. Is this a property of 2PC as defined in item 2 and item 3?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

No. With prepared participants that wait for the decision, a coordinator crash leaves them in doubt but never deciding differently: the weakness is
blocking, not inconsistency, as Tan's next page says. Inconsistency appears only in variants where an in-doubt participant decides by timeout.

## Python

A coordinator crash with waiting participants and with timing-out ones.

```{.python .run}
def outcome(policy):
    decided = {"A": "commit"}                    # A received commit before the crash
    decided["B"] = "waiting" if policy == "wait" else "abort"
    return decided
print("wait:", outcome("wait"), "| timeout to abort:", outcome("timeout"))
```

```{.text .run-output}
wait: {'A': 'commit', 'B': 'waiting'} | timeout to abort: {'A': 'commit', 'B': 'abort'}
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise counts messages. Two round trips per participant.

::: {#exr-ac-messages}
#### Messages per transaction

Count the messages of a committed 2PC transaction with $n$ participants and a separate coordinator, and the forced log writes before the client learns
the outcome.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Prepare, vote, decision and acknowledgement for each participant: $4n$ messages. Each participant forces its prepared record and the coordinator its
decision: $n + 1$ forced writes before the decision is sent; the acknowledgements and the participants' commit records can follow.

## Python

The counts.

```{.python .run}
for n in (2, 3, 10): print(n, "participants:", 4 * n, "messages,", n + 1, "forced writes")
```

```{.text .run-output}
2 participants: 8 messages, 3 forced writes
3 participants: 12 messages, 4 forced writes
10 participants: 40 messages, 11 forced writes
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise asks what an operator should do with a participant in doubt for hours. Any choice is a guess.

::: {#exr-ac-heuristic}
#### Deciding by hand

The coordinator's disk is lost and a participant has been in doubt for three hours, holding locks. Tan notes that "crash recovery and synchronization
must be done manually" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, App. D, p. 421]. What information settles the decision, and what if none is available?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

If any participant has committed, the decision was commit; if any voted no or never voted, the decision was abort. If every reachable participant is in doubt, the outcome is unknown: an operator who commits or aborts may contradict a participant that
cannot be reached, so the result must be reconciled afterwards.

## Python

The rule from participants' states.

```{.python .run}
def infer(states):
    if "committed" in states: return "commit"
    if "aborted" in states or "not voted" in states: return "abort"
    return "unknown"
for st in (["in doubt", "committed"], ["in doubt", "not voted"], ["in doubt", "in doubt"]): print(st, "->", infer(st))
```

```{.text .run-output}
['in doubt', 'committed'] -> commit
['in doubt', 'not voted'] -> abort
['in doubt', 'in doubt'] -> unknown
```
::::
:::

::::

### Safety, blocking and cost

Two-phase commit never lets participants disagree, but it can leave them waiting. The theorem proves both, counts its cost, and shows how replicating
the coordinator removes the wait.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-two-phase-commit}
#### Two-phase commit: safety, blocking and cost

Let processes crash and recover with their logs intact, let messages be lost or delayed but not altered, let participants log their votes before sending
them, and let the coordinator log its decision, once, before sending it.

(a) In every run of 2PC, agreement and validity hold, and non-triviality holds in runs without failures or lost messages.

(b) No rule by which in-doubt participants decide without hearing from the coordinator can guarantee agreement. Precisely: if the coordinator and one
participant $p_1$ are unreachable and the other participants are all in doubt, the runs in which the decision was commit and in which it was abort can look
the same to them.

(c) A committed transaction with $n$ participants and a separate coordinator takes $4n$ messages and $n + 1$ forced log writes before the decision is
sent, and at least two round trips between coordinator and participants.

(d) If the decision is the value decided by a consensus group of $2f + 1$ replicas (@def-consensus), an in-doubt participant learns it from the group
whenever at most $f$ replicas of the group have failed and the group can communicate: the crash of one coordinator no longer blocks.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) A participant decides commit only on receiving commit, and the coordinator sends commit only after logging it, which it does only after
receiving yes from every participant; so commit implies that all voted yes, which is validity. A participant decides abort on receiving abort, or by
itself before voting, in which case it never sends yes and the coordinator, lacking its vote, cannot decide commit. The coordinator decides once, logs the
decision before sending it, and after recovery resends the logged decision, so all decisions it sends are the same. Hence every participant that decides
commit and every one that decides abort follows the one decision, or, for an abort before voting, a run where the decision cannot be commit: agreement. In
a run without failures every yes arrives and commit is decided and delivered: non-triviality.

(b) Consider two runs. In the first, every participant votes yes, the coordinator decides commit and sends it to $p_1$, which commits; then the coordinator
and $p_1$ become unreachable. In the second, $p_1$ votes no and aborts; the coordinator decides abort and sends it to $p_1$ only, and then both become
unreachable. The other participants voted yes in both runs and received nothing after their votes, so their logs and messages are identical in the two.
A rule that decides from this information decides the same in both runs, disagreeing with $p_1$ in one of them.

(c) Each participant receives a prepare request and sends a vote, then receives the decision and sends an acknowledgement: $4n$ messages. Each prepared
participant forces its prepared record before voting, and the coordinator forces its decision before sending it: $n + 1$ writes. The decision can be sent
only after a prepare has gone out and every vote has come back, one round trip, and it reaches the participants after a further half round trip; the
acknowledgements complete the second.

(d) By agreement of consensus all replicas that decide the transaction's outcome decide the same value, and by validity it is a value proposed by the
coordinator, commit only after all yes votes; so (a) still holds. By @prp-consensus-quorums (b) a majority of the group remains after $f$ crashes, and by
termination it decides; an in-doubt participant that asks a majority receives the decided value, since by @prp-consensus-quorums (a) that majority
intersects the majority that accepted it. $\square$

Part (b) is the formal content of Tan's "the coordinator must be available throughout the process". Part (d) is how Spanner answers it: "Running
two-phase commit over Paxos mitigates the availability problems" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 2.3].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Part (a) and (b) in many runs. Coordinators crash at random points; participants wait.

::: {#exm-tpc-sim}
#### Crashes in a seeded simulation

Ten thousand transactions with three participants: votes fail with probability $0.05$ and the coordinator crashes before sending its decision with
probability $0.02$. No run ends with participants disagreeing; the runs with a crash leave participants in doubt until the coordinator recovers.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(31)
disagree = blocked = committed = 0
for _ in range(10000):
    votes = [random.random() > 0.05 for _ in range(3)]
    decision = "commit" if all(votes) else "abort"
    crash = random.random() < 0.02
    states = []
    for v in votes:
        if not v: states.append("abort")                 # voted no: aborts at once
        elif crash: states.append("in doubt")
        else: states.append(decision)
    final = {s for s in states if s != "in doubt"}
    disagree += len(final) > 1
    blocked += "in doubt" in states
    committed += states == ["commit"] * 3
print("disagreements", disagree, "| runs with participants in doubt", blocked, "| committed", committed)
```

```{.text .run-output}
disagreements 0 | runs with participants in doubt 197 | committed 8421
```
:::

The proof's two runs, side by side. The waiting participants see the same thing in both.

::: {#exm-tpc-blocking-run}
#### The two runs of part (b)

What participants $p_2$ and $p_3$ observe is printed for both runs: identical, although the decisions differ.

```{.python .run}
def run(p1_vote):
    decision = "commit" if p1_vote else "abort"
    seen_by_others = {"own vote": "yes", "messages after voting": []}
    return decision, seen_by_others
a, b = run(True), run(False)
print("decisions:", a[0], b[0], "| observations equal:", a[1] == b[1])
```

```{.text .run-output}
decisions: commit abort | observations equal: True
```
:::

Part (c) for the photo service's two stores. Eight messages and three forced writes.

::: {#exm-tpc-cost}
#### Cost of a commit

With $n = 2$, a commit takes $8$ messages and $3$ forced writes; with round trips of $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ and writes of $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ the decision is sent
after about $3\,\mathrm{ms}$, a prepare round and two writes in sequence.

```{.python .run}
n, rtt, w = 2, 1.0, 1.0
print(4 * n, "messages,", n + 1, "forced writes, decision after", rtt + w + w, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
8 messages, 3 forced writes, decision after 3.0 ms
```
:::

Spanner's participants are Paxos groups. Part (d) is its design.

::: {#exm-tpc-spanner}
#### Two-phase commit over Paxos

Each participant "logs a prepare record through Paxos", and the coordinator leader "logs a commit record through Paxos (or an abort if it timed out
while waiting on the other participants)" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.1]: every record of the protocol is a value decided by a replicated group, so the
crash of one leader does not lose it.
:::

Liu states part (b) in one line. The service is unavailable while the coordinator is.

::: {#exm-tpc-liu}
#### The coordinator is down

"The challenge of 2PC is that if the coordinator is down, the service becomes unavailable" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Distributed
Transaction"]: in-doubt participants hold their locks, and new transactions cannot start without a coordinator.
:::

Part (d) with the photo metadata's cluster. Five replicas survive two failures.

::: {#exm-tpc-groups}
#### How large a group

A coordinator group of $5$ replicas in three zones, as the metadata cluster of the consistency chapter, decides outcomes while at most $2$ replicas are
down; a single coordinator of availability $0.999$ blocks $0.1\%$ of the time, the group, with independent replicas, about $10^{-8}$.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
a = 0.999
group = sum(comb(5, k) * a ** k * (1 - a) ** (5 - k) for k in range(3, 6))
print(f"single coordinator unavailable {1 - a:.0e}, group of 5 unavailable {1 - group:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
single coordinator unavailable 1e-03, group of 5 unavailable 1.0e-08
```
:::

Validity covers a participant that refuses at the last moment. The coordinator cannot commit without it.

::: {#exm-tpc-validity}
#### A no vote after a long wait

A participant whose disk is full votes no; the other votes yes and waits. The coordinator decides abort, and the waiting participant discards its
prepared part: part (a)'s validity.
:::

Part (c)'s round trips dominate across regions. Spanner lets the client drive the protocol to save one transfer.

::: {#exm-tpc-latency}
#### Latency over wide-area links

With participants $50\,\mathrm{ms}$ apart, two round trips are $100\,\mathrm{ms}$ before forced writes. Spanner notes that "having the client drive two-phase
commit avoids sending data twice across wide-area links" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.1].
:::

The coordinator may abort when a vote is late. That keeps the coordinator from blocking.

::: {#exm-tpc-timeout}
#### Timeouts before the decision

Spanner's coordinator logs "an abort if it timed out while waiting on the other participants" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.1]. A late vote is treated
as no; validity holds, since commit still needs every yes, and non-triviality only promises commit when nothing fails.
:::

Gilbert's objection and part (b) are different. Part (d) answers one, not the other.

::: {#exm-tpc-gilbert-scale}
#### Scale and blocking

Replicating the coordinator removes blocking on its crash but not the cost of part (c) or the need for every participant to be available, which Gilbert
and Tan object to (@exm-ac-gilbert, @exm-ac-tan-services).
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks part (a) by simulation with recovery. Crashed coordinators recover and resend their logged decisions.

::: {#exr-tpc-agreement-check}
#### Agreement under random failures

Simulate 2PC with crashes of the coordinator before or after logging, recovery after a while, and lost decision messages that are resent. Check that every
participant that decides, decides the same.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (a) agreement holds in every run; the simulation, which follows the rules of item 2 and the coordinator's recovery of @exr-ac-recovery, finds no
violation, and every run ends decided once the coordinator recovers.

## Python

Seeded runs.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(32)
bad = undecided = 0
for _ in range(20000):
    votes = [random.random() > 0.03 for _ in range(4)]
    log = None
    if random.random() < 0.1: pass                     # crash before logging: recovery decides abort
    else: log = "commit" if all(votes) else "abort"
    decision = log or "abort"                           # after recovery
    states = [("abort" if not v else decision) for v in votes]
    bad += len(set(states)) > 1 and "commit" in states
print("runs with disagreement:", bad)
```

```{.text .run-output}
runs with disagreement: 0
```
::::
:::

The second exercise tries concrete rules for in-doubt participants. Each fails in one of the two runs.

::: {#exr-tpc-three-runs}
#### Part (b) with any rule

Try three rules for in-doubt participants who can reach each other but not the coordinator or $p_1$: always commit, always abort, and commit after a
timeout if all reachable participants voted yes. Show each fails in a run of part (b).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

All three see the same thing in both runs. "Always commit" and "commit if all reachable voted yes" disagree with $p_1$ in the second run, where $p_1$
aborted; "always abort" disagrees with $p_1$ in the first, where it committed.

## Python

Each rule in both runs.

```{.python .run}
rules = {"always commit": "commit", "always abort": "abort", "commit if reachable voted yes": "commit"}
for name, d in rules.items():
    print(name, "| run 1 (p1 committed):", "ok" if d == "commit" else "DISAGREES",
          "| run 2 (p1 aborted):", "ok" if d == "abort" else "DISAGREES")
```

```{.text .run-output}
always commit | run 1 (p1 committed): ok | run 2 (p1 aborted): DISAGREES
always abort | run 1 (p1 committed): DISAGREES | run 2 (p1 aborted): ok
commit if reachable voted yes | run 1 (p1 committed): ok | run 2 (p1 aborted): DISAGREES
```
::::
:::

The third exercise prices part (b) with a single coordinator. Blocking lasts as long as the coordinator's repair.

::: {#exr-tpc-blocking-duration}
#### Expected blocking

The coordinator crashes in a transaction's in-doubt window with probability $10^{-5}$ and takes $10$ minutes to recover. At $100$ transactions per second,
how many transactions block a day, and for how many lock-minutes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$8.64 \times 10^6 \times 10^{-5} = 86$ crashes' worth of transactions a day, each blocking its locks for $10$ minutes: $864$ lock-minutes. A crash also blocks
every transaction then in doubt, so the count is a lower bound.

## Python

The products.

```{.python .run}
n = 100 * 86400
print(f"{n * 1e-5:.0f} blocked transactions, {n * 1e-5 * 10:.0f} lock-minutes")
```

```{.text .run-output}
86 blocked transactions, 864 lock-minutes
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise drops the acknowledgements of part (c). The coordinator must then keep its log entry.

::: {#exr-tpc-count}
#### Messages without acknowledgements

If participants do not acknowledge the decision, how many messages does a commit take, and why does the coordinator then need to keep the decision in its
log indefinitely?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$3n$. The acknowledgements tell the coordinator that no participant can ask again, so it can forget the decision; without them it must keep every decision,
since a recovering participant may ask about any transaction.

## Python

The counts.

```{.python .run}
for n in (2, 5): print(n, "with acks", 4 * n, "| without", 3 * n)
```

```{.text .run-output}
2 with acks 8 | without 6
5 with acks 20 | without 15
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise checks part (d)'s intersection. A participant reading any majority finds the decision.

::: {#exr-tpc-majority}
#### The group's majority

A group of $5$ replicas has accepted the decision at a majority. Check that every majority of the $5$ contains at least one replica that accepted it, for all
$\binom{5}{3}$ accepting majorities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By @prp-consensus-quorums (a), two majorities of $5$ share at least $3 + 3 - 5 = 1$ replica; the check enumerates all pairs.

## Python

All pairs of majorities.

```{.python .run}
from itertools import combinations
majorities = [set(c) for k in (3, 4, 5) for c in combinations(range(5), k)]
print("every pair intersects:", all(a & b for a in majorities for b in majorities))
```

```{.text .run-output}
every pair intersects: True
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise lets in-doubt participants ask each other. It sometimes ends the wait, but not always.

::: {#exr-tpc-cooperative}
#### Asking the other participants

An in-doubt participant asks the others. When can it decide from their answers, and why does this not contradict part (b)?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

If any other participant has committed or aborted, or has not voted (and so will vote no), the decision follows, as in @exr-ac-heuristic. If every reachable
participant is in doubt, it must wait: that is exactly part (b)'s situation, where an unreachable $p_1$ holds the only information.

## Python

The cases.

```{.python .run}
def ask(others):
    if "committed" in others: return "commit"
    if "aborted" in others or "not voted" in others: return "abort"
    return "wait"
for o in (["in doubt", "committed"], ["in doubt", "not voted"], ["in doubt", "in doubt"]): print(o, "->", ask(o))
```

```{.text .run-output}
['in doubt', 'committed'] -> commit
['in doubt', 'not voted'] -> abort
['in doubt', 'in doubt'] -> wait
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise turns part (c) into milliseconds. Writes and round trips are in sequence.

::: {#exr-tpc-latency}
#### Latency of a commit

With a round trip of $r$ between coordinator and participants and forced writes of $w$, find the time from the start of prepare to the participants' receipt of
the decision. Evaluate for $r = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, $w = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$ and for $r = 60\,\mathrm{ms}$, $w = 5\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Prepare travels $r/2$, participants write ($w$) and vote ($r/2$), the coordinator writes ($w$) and the decision travels $r/2$: $3r/2 + 2w$. That is $3.5\,\mathrm{ms}$
and $100\,\mathrm{ms}$.

## Python

Both settings.

```{.python .run}
for r, w in ((1, 1), (60, 5)): print(f"r={r}, w={w}: {1.5 * r + 2 * w} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
r=1, w=1: 3.5 ms
r=60, w=5: 100.0 ms
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise lets a participant skip the second phase. It has nothing to commit.

::: {#exr-tpc-read-only}
#### A participant that only read

A participant only read data in the transaction. Show that it can vote yes and release its locks at once, without waiting for the decision, and that agreement
is not affected.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It has no changes, so commit and abort have the same effect on its state; nothing it does can disagree with the decision. It can release its read locks after
voting, and the coordinator need not send it the decision: one round trip and one forced write saved.

## Python

Messages saved by $k$ read-only participants among $n$.

```{.python .run}
n, k = 5, 2
print("messages:", 4 * n, "->", 4 * n - 2 * k)
```

```{.text .run-output}
messages: 20 -> 16
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise reads Liu's phrase about the second phase. Retrying the decision is what makes agreement durable.

::: {#exr-tpc-liu-push}
#### Pushing the second phase

Liu: "the coordinator will continue to push the 2nd phase commit until they go through". Which part of the theorem needs this, and what assumption makes
it terminate?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Agreement holds without it, but a participant that never receives the decision stays in doubt; resending the logged decision until acknowledged ends the
doubt. It terminates if the participant eventually recovers and messages are eventually delivered, as part (a)'s assumptions allow.

## Python

Resending until delivered, with a loss probability of $0.3$.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(33)
tries = []
for _ in range(10000):
    t = 1
    while random.random() < 0.3: t += 1
    tries.append(t)
print("mean sends", round(sum(tries) / len(tries), 3), "| expected", round(1 / 0.7, 3))
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean sends 1.431 | expected 1.429
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise compares the coordinator's unavailability with and without part (d). Independence decides the gain.

::: {#exr-tpc-why-group}
#### One coordinator or a group

A coordinator machine is unavailable $0.1\%$ of the time. Find how often a group of $3$ and of $5$ such machines lacks a majority, if they fail independently.
Why is independence the important assumption?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With $a = 0.999$: $3$ machines lack a majority with probability $3 \times 10^{-6}$, $5$ machines with about $10^{-8}$. If the machines share a power supply or a
zone, their failures are correlated and the gain disappears; the groups of the consistency chapter are spread across zones for this reason.

## Python

Binomial tails.

```{.python .run}
from math import comb
a = 0.999
for n in (3, 5):
    up = sum(comb(n, k) * a ** k * (1 - a) ** (n - k) for k in range(n // 2 + 1, n + 1))
    print(n, f"{1 - up:.1e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
3 3.0e-06
5 1.0e-08
```
::::
:::

::::

## Global time and Spanner {#sec-spanner}

Logical clocks order events that can affect each other through the system (@thm-logical-clocks), but not events linked outside it, such as a user who
writes on one server and then telephones a friend who reads on another. Lamport called the resulting surprises "anomalous behavior" and showed that
synchronised physical clocks remove them [@lamport1978time, p. 562]. Spanner builds on such clocks: it "assigns globally-meaningful commit timestamps to
transactions, even though transactions may be distributed" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 1]. This section defines physical clocks, TrueTime and external
consistency, and proves that Spanner's commit wait makes transactions externally consistent.

For more on this topic, see @lamport1978time [pp. 562-563, "Physical Clocks"] and @corbett2012spanner [Secs. 3 and 4.1-4.2].

### Physical clocks, TrueTime and external consistency

A clock with a known error bound can say when a time has certainly passed. Spanner waits until it has, as @fig-tt-wait shows.

![Commit wait: the commit timestamp is the latest end of the clock's interval when the commit request arrives, and the data become visible once the earliest
end of a later interval passes it. With a constant uncertainty the wait is twice the uncertainty.](figures/commit_wait.svg){#fig-tt-wait width=80%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-truetime}
#### Physical clocks, TrueTime and external consistency

1. A **physical clock** $C_i$ is a function of physical time $t$, continuous and increasing except where it is set forward. Its **drift** is bounded by
   $\kappa$ if $|dC_i(t)/dt - 1| < \kappa$, and clocks $C_i$, $C_j$ have **skew** bounded by $\varepsilon$ if $|C_i(t) - C_j(t)| < \varepsilon$ for all $t$
   (Lamport's conditions PC1 and PC2).
2. The **strong clock condition** holds for a set of events, including events outside the system such as telephone calls, if $a$ happening before $b$ in
   that set implies $C(a) < C(b)$.
3. **TrueTime** returns, for a call at absolute time $t$, an interval $\mathrm{TT.now}() = [\mathit{earliest}, \mathit{latest}]$ with
   $\mathit{earliest} \leq t \leq \mathit{latest}$; its **uncertainty** $\varepsilon$ is half the interval's width. $\mathrm{TT.after}(s)$ is true if $s$ has
   certainly passed, $s < \mathit{earliest}$, and $\mathrm{TT.before}(s)$ if $s$ has certainly not arrived, $\mathit{latest} < s$.
4. Transactions with commit timestamps $s_i$ are **externally consistent** if whenever $T_1$ commits before $T_2$ starts, in absolute time, $s_1 < s_2$.
   Spanner's **start rule** gives a read-write transaction a commit timestamp $s \geq \mathrm{TT.now}().\mathit{latest}$, computed after its commit request
   arrives at the coordinator; its **commit wait** keeps clients from seeing the transaction's data until $\mathrm{TT.after}(s)$ is true.
:::

::::

Items 1 and 2 are Lamport's [@lamport1978time, pp. 562-563], with $\kappa$ and $\varepsilon$ in his notation. Items 3 and 4 are Spanner's: TrueTime
"guarantees that for an invocation tt = TT.now(), tt.earliest ≤ tabs(enow) ≤ tt.latest", and external consistency means that "if the start of a transaction
$T_2$ occurs after the commit of a transaction $T_1$, then the commit timestamp of $T_2$ must be greater than the commit timestamp of $T_1$"
[@corbett2012spanner, Secs. 3 and 4.1.2]. Spanner calls this property equivalent to linearisability [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 1], the strongest model
of @def-consistency-models.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Lamport's example of anomalous behaviour is a phone call. Logical clocks cannot see it.

::: {#exm-tt-phone}
#### The telephone call

A person issues request $A$ on one computer, "then telephones a friend in another city to have him issue a request B on a different computer B. It is
quite possible for request B to receive a lower timestamp and be ordered before request A ... the system has no way of knowing that A actually preceded B"
[@lamport1978time, p. 562]. In the photo service: a user uploads a photo, then tells a friend, whose feed read must include it.
:::

Lamport gives two ways out. The first makes the user carry the timestamp.

::: {#exm-tt-two-ways}
#### Two remedies

"The person issuing request A could receive the timestamp $T_A$ of that request from the system. When issuing request B, his friend could specify that B be
given a timestamp later than $T_A$. This gives the user the responsibility for avoiding anomalous behavior. The second approach is to construct a system of
clocks which satisfies" the strong clock condition [@lamport1978time, p. 562]. A session token carrying the last write's timestamp is the first remedy;
TrueTime is the second.
:::

Lamport's drift bound for ordinary clocks is about a microsecond per second. Over a day it adds up.

::: {#exm-tt-crystal}
#### Drift of a crystal clock

"For typical crystal controlled clocks, $\kappa \leq 10^{-6}$" [@lamport1978time, p. 563]. Two such clocks drifting in opposite directions separate by up to
$2 \times 10^{-6} \times 86400 = 0.17\,\mathrm{s}$ a day, so they must be resynchronised regularly to keep $\varepsilon$ small.

```{.python .run}
kappa = 1e-6
print(f"separation per day: {2 * kappa * 86400:.3f} s, per 30 s: {2 * kappa * 30 * 1e6:.0f} microseconds")
```

```{.text .run-output}
separation per day: 0.173 s, per 30 s: 60 microseconds
```
:::

TrueTime's uncertainty is a sawtooth. Spanner gives its parts.

::: {#exm-tt-spanner-eps}
#### Spanner's uncertainty

Between synchronisations a daemon "advertises a slowly increasing time uncertainty"; "the daemon's poll interval is currently 30 seconds, and the current
applied drift rate is set at 200 microseconds/second, which together account for the sawtooth bounds from 0 to 6 ms. The remaining 1 ms comes from the
communication delay to the time masters", so $\varepsilon$ varies "from about 1 to 7 ms over each poll interval" and is $4\,\mathrm{ms}$ on average
[@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 3]. $200\,\mu\mathrm{s/s} \times 30\,\mathrm{s} = 6\,\mathrm{ms}$.

```{.python .run}
drift, poll, comm = 200e-6, 30, 1e-3
print(f"sawtooth top {drift * poll * 1e3:.0f} ms, range {comm * 1e3:.0f}-{(comm + drift * poll) * 1e3:.0f} ms, mean {(comm + drift * poll / 2) * 1e3:.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
sawtooth top 6 ms, range 1-7 ms, mean 4 ms
```
:::

TrueTime uses GPS and atomic clocks. They fail differently.

::: {#exm-tt-sources}
#### Two kinds of time reference

"TrueTime uses two forms of time reference because they have different failure modes. GPS reference-source vulnerabilities include antenna and receiver
failures, local radio interference, correlated failures ... Atomic clocks can fail in ways uncorrelated to GPS and each other, and over long periods of time
can drift significantly due to frequency error" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 3].
:::

Item 3's interface is three functions. A simulated clock with known error gives them.

::: {#exm-tt-interval}
#### An interval in code

A machine whose clock is $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ fast with uncertainty $\varepsilon = 4\,\mathrm{ms}$ returns intervals that still contain the true time.

```{.python .run}
true_t, offset, eps = 100.000, 0.002, 0.004
reading = true_t + offset
earliest, latest = reading - eps, reading + eps
after = lambda s: s < earliest
before = lambda s: latest < s
print(f"[{earliest:.3f}, {latest:.3f}] contains {true_t}: {earliest <= true_t <= latest};",
      "after(99.99):", after(99.99), "before(100.01):", before(100.01))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[99.998, 100.006] contains 100.0: True; after(99.99): True before(100.01): True
```
:::

Item 4 is what the phone call needs. The friend's read starts after the upload commits.

::: {#exm-tt-external}
#### External consistency for the photo feed

If the upload's transaction $T_1$ commits before the friend's read transaction $T_2$ starts, external consistency gives $s_1 < s_2$, so a read at $s_2$ sees
the photo, whichever servers are involved.
:::

Spanner also keeps timestamps increasing inside each Paxos group. Leases make it hold across leaders.

::: {#exm-tt-monotonic}
#### Timestamps within a group

"Within each Paxos group, Spanner assigns timestamps to Paxos writes in monotonically increasing order, even across leaders ... This invariant is enforced
across leaders by making use of the disjointness invariant: a leader must only assign timestamps within the interval of its leader lease"
[@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.1.2]: the leases of @def-coordination, used for time.
:::

Timestamps let reads avoid locks. A read at a past timestamp sees a consistent snapshot.

::: {#exm-tt-reads}
#### Reads without locks

Spanner lists "lock-free read-only transactions" and "non-blocking reads in the past" among the features TrueTime enables [@corbett2012spanner,
Abstract and Sec. 4]: a read at timestamp $s$ returns every write with timestamp at most $s$ and none after, the snapshot of @def-transaction-isolation at a
chosen time.
:::

A larger uncertainty makes Spanner slower, not incorrect. The paper says so directly.

::: {#exm-tt-slow}
#### Uncertainty costs time

"The guarantees on Spanner's timestamps depend on the bounds that the implementation provides. If the uncertainty is large, Spanner slows down to wait out
that uncertainty" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 1].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the anomaly with Lamport clocks. The clocks satisfy their condition and still misorder the requests.

::: {#exr-tt-logical}
#### Logical clocks and the phone call

Server $A$ has Lamport clock $50$ and server $B$ clock $10$, with no messages between them. Request $A$ happens on $A$, then, after a phone call, request $B$ on $B$.
What timestamps do they get, and which condition of @def-truetime fails?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$A$ gets $51$, $B$ gets $11$: $B$ is ordered first. The clock condition of @thm-logical-clocks holds, since no message relates the events; the strong
clock condition of item 2 fails, because the phone call is outside the system.

## Python

The two clocks.

```{.python .run}
clock = {"A": 50, "B": 10}
def event(s): clock[s] += 1; return clock[s]
tA = event("A"); tB = event("B")           # B happens after A, via a phone call
print("A:", tA, "B:", tB, "| ordered first:", "B" if tB < tA else "A")
```

```{.text .run-output}
A: 51 B: 11 | ordered first: B
```
::::
:::

The second exercise turns drift into a polling interval. Skew grows twice as fast as one clock drifts.

::: {#exr-tt-resync}
#### How often to resynchronise

Two clocks of drift bound $\kappa = 10^{-5}$ are reset to agree. How long until their skew can reach $1\,\mathrm{ms}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each can run up to $\kappa$ fast or slow, so their difference grows at most $2\kappa$ per second: $10^{-3}/(2 \times 10^{-5}) = 50\,\mathrm{s}$.

## Python

The quotient.

```{.python .run}
print(1e-3 / (2 * 1e-5), "s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
50.0 s
```
::::
:::

The third exercise simulates item 3's guarantee. Readings with bounded error give intervals that always contain the true time.

::: {#exr-tt-contains}
#### Intervals that contain the time

Clocks read the true time with an error uniform in $[-\varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_0]$, $\varepsilon_0 = 3\,\mathrm{ms}$. Show that intervals of half-width
$\varepsilon_0$ always contain the true time, and that half-width $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ fails sometimes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$|reading - t| \leq \varepsilon_0$ is exactly $t \in [reading - \varepsilon_0, reading + \varepsilon_0]$. With a smaller half-width the guarantee fails whenever
the error exceeds it, here a third of the time.

## Python

A simulation.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(34)
err = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 100000)
for half in (3, 2): print(half, "ms: contains the time", f"{(np.abs(err) <= half).mean():.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
3 ms: contains the time 1.000
2 ms: contains the time 0.667
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise classifies a timestamp against an interval. Inside the interval, neither function is true.

::: {#exr-tt-after-before}
#### After, before and neither

With $\mathrm{TT.now}() = [10.000, 10.008]$, evaluate $\mathrm{TT.after}(s)$ and $\mathrm{TT.before}(s)$ for $s = 9.99$, $10.004$ and $10.02$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$9.99$: after true, before false. $10.004$: both false, the time may or may not have passed. $10.02$: after false, before true.

## Python

The three cases.

```{.python .run}
e, l = 10.000, 10.008
for s in (9.99, 10.004, 10.02): print(s, "after", s < e, "before", l < s)
```

```{.text .run-output}
9.99 after True before False
10.004 after False before False
10.02 after False before True
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise drops commit wait. A transaction can then become visible before its timestamp.

::: {#exr-tt-without-wait}
#### External consistency without waiting

A coordinator assigns $s_1 = \mathrm{TT.now}().\mathit{latest} = 10.008$ at true time $10.004$ and makes the data visible at once. A client reads it, then starts $T_2$
on a server whose interval at true time $10.005$ is $[10.001, 10.007]$, which assigns $s_2 = 10.007$. Is item 4 violated?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Yes: $T_1$ committed (became visible) before $T_2$ started, but $s_2 = 10.007 < s_1 = 10.008$. Commit wait would have delayed $T_1$'s visibility until
earliest exceeds $10.008$, at true time at least $10.008$, after which any $\mathit{latest}$ is larger.

## Python

The two timestamps.

```{.python .run}
s1, s2 = 10.008, 10.007
print("s1 < s2:", s1 < s2)
```

```{.text .run-output}
s1 < s2: False
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise reads at a past timestamp. It needs only the versions with smaller timestamps.

::: {#exr-tt-reads-past}
#### A snapshot read

A row has versions with timestamps $3$, $7$ and $12$. What does a read at $s = 10$ return, and why need it not take locks?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The version of $7$, the newest at or before $10$. By external consistency every transaction with timestamp below $10$ that will ever be visible has already
committed once $\mathrm{TT.after}(10)$ holds, so the versions up to $10$ no longer change, and nothing needs to be locked.

## Python

A versioned lookup.

```{.python .run}
import bisect
versions = [(3, "a"), (7, "b"), (12, "c")]
ts = [t for t, _ in versions]
print(versions[bisect.bisect_right(ts, 10) - 1])
```

```{.text .run-output}
(7, 'b')
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise breaks TrueTime's assumption. Spanner evicts such machines.

::: {#exr-tt-bad-clock}
#### A clock that drifts too fast

TrueTime assumes drift at most $200\,\mu\mathrm{s/s}$. A machine drifts at $500\,\mu\mathrm{s/s}$ for $30\,\mathrm{s}$ after synchronising. By how much can its true
error exceed the advertised uncertainty, and what does Spanner do about such machines?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It advertises $6\,\mathrm{ms}$ of drift uncertainty but may be $15\,\mathrm{ms}$ off: $9\,\mathrm{ms}$ outside its interval, breaking item 3 and hence the theorem's
guarantee. Spanner evicts "machines that exhibit frequency excursions larger than the worst-case bound", and reports that "bad CPUs are 6 times more likely than
bad clocks" [@corbett2012spanner, Secs. 3 and 5.3].

## Python

The two errors.

```{.python .run}
print("advertised", 200e-6 * 30 * 1e3, "ms; actual", 500e-6 * 30 * 1e3, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
advertised 6.0 ms; actual 15.0 ms
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise reads Spanner's TrueTime measurements. Tails, not means, set the worst commit waits.

::: {#exr-tt-percentiles}
#### Uncertainty in the tail

Spanner reports that "the base value of $\varepsilon$ [is] generally not a problem. However, there can be significant tail-latency issues that cause higher values
of $\varepsilon$", and an hour-long increase when "2 time masters at a datacenter" were shut down [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 5.3]. If commit wait is about
$2\varepsilon$, what does a spike from $4$ to $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ do to a $15\,\mathrm{ms}$ write?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The wait grows from about $8$ to $20\,\mathrm{ms}$, so if the wait is not overlapped with replication the write grows from $15$ to about $27\,\mathrm{ms}$: correctness is
untouched, latency follows $\varepsilon$.

## Python

The two latencies, without overlap.

```{.python .run}
base = 15 - 2 * 4
for eps in (4, 10): print(eps, "ms uncertainty:", base + 2 * eps, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
4 ms uncertainty: 15 ms
10 ms uncertainty: 27 ms
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise implements the user-carried timestamp. It needs no synchronised clocks.

::: {#exr-tt-user-token}
#### Lamport's first remedy

Implement Lamport's first remedy for the photo service: the upload returns its timestamp, and the friend's read must be served at a timestamp at least as
large. Show it gives the order of the phone call even with skewed clocks.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The read carries $T_A$ and the serving server advances its clock past $T_A$ before serving, as Lamport clocks do on receiving a message
(@thm-logical-clocks): the phone call has become a message.

## Python

Two servers with skewed clocks.

```{.python .run}
clock = {"A": 50, "B": 10}
tA = clock["A"] = clock["A"] + 1
token = tA                                    # told to the friend with the phone call
clock["B"] = max(clock["B"], token) + 1
print("A", tA, "B", clock["B"], "| B after A:", clock["B"] > tA)
```

```{.text .run-output}
A 51 B 52 | B after A: True
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise asks when commit wait is free. It overlaps with the Paxos round.

::: {#exr-tt-wait-cost}
#### Waiting overlapped with replication

Spanner writes that "this wait is typically overlapped with Paxos communication" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.1], and measured a commit wait of about
$5\,\mathrm{ms}$ and a Paxos latency of about $9\,\mathrm{ms}$ [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 5.1]. What does the wait add to a write, with and without overlap?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Overlapped, the write takes $\max(5, 9) = 9\,\mathrm{ms}$ and the wait adds nothing; in sequence, $14\,\mathrm{ms}$. Commit wait costs latency only when it is longer than
the replication it runs beside.

## Python

Both.

```{.python .run}
wait, paxos = 5, 9
print("overlapped", max(wait, paxos), "ms; sequential", wait + paxos, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
overlapped 9 ms; sequential 14 ms
```
::::
:::

::::

### Why commit wait gives external consistency

The start rule puts the timestamp after the request's arrival, and commit wait puts the visibility after the timestamp. Together they order transactions as
absolute time does.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-commit-wait}
#### Commit wait and physical clocks

(a) If read-write transactions follow the start rule and commit wait of @def-truetime, and a transaction starts no earlier than its commit request can arrive
at its coordinator, then the transactions are externally consistent.

(b) If every call $\mathrm{TT.now}()$ at absolute time $t$ returns $[t - \varepsilon, t + \varepsilon]$ and the coordinator takes $s = \mathrm{TT.now}().\mathit{latest}$,
commit wait lasts $2\varepsilon$. If calls return any intervals of half-width at most $\varepsilon_{\max}$, it lasts at most $4\varepsilon_{\max}$.

(c) (Lamport) If physical clocks satisfy PC1 with $\kappa < 1$ and PC2 with $\varepsilon$, are never set back, and every relation $a \to b$ between events of
different processes, inside or outside the system, takes at least $\mu$ of physical time, then $\varepsilon/(1 - \kappa) \leq \mu$ implies the strong clock
condition for events of different processes.

(d) (Lamport, quoted) In a strongly connected network of diameter $d$ whose processes follow his rules IR1' and IR2', in which PC1 holds and every
$\tau$ seconds a message with unpredictable delay less than $\xi$ is sent over every arc, "PC2 is satisfied with $\varepsilon \approx d(2\kappa\tau + \xi)$ for all
$t \gtrsim t_0 + \tau d$, where the approximations assume $\mu + \xi \ll \tau$" [@lamport1978time, p. 563]. The proof is in Lamport's appendix and is not
reproduced here.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) Let $T_1$ commit before $T_2$ starts, and write $t(\cdot)$ for absolute times; let $e^{\mathrm{server}}_2$ be the arrival of $T_2$'s commit request
at its coordinator. Commit wait makes $T_1$'s data visible only once $\mathrm{TT.after}(s_1)$ holds, at some time $t$ with $s_1 < \mathit{earliest} \leq t$;
so $s_1 < t(e^{\mathrm{commit}}_1)$. By assumption $t(e^{\mathrm{commit}}_1) < t(e^{\mathrm{start}}_2) \leq t(e^{\mathrm{server}}_2)$. By the start rule
$s_2 \geq \mathit{latest} \geq t(e^{\mathrm{server}}_2)$ for the interval computed after $e^{\mathrm{server}}_2$. Chaining, $s_1 < s_2$. This is Spanner's
proof [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.1.2].

(b) Symmetric intervals: $s = t_0 + \varepsilon$ for the call at $t_0$, and $\mathrm{TT.after}(s)$ holds at $t$ when $t - \varepsilon > s$, that is $t > t_0 + 2\varepsilon$.
General intervals: $\mathit{latest} \leq t_0 + 2\varepsilon_{\max}$, since the interval contains $t_0$ and has width at most $2\varepsilon_{\max}$; and at time $t$,
$\mathit{earliest} \geq t - 2\varepsilon_{\max}$, so $\mathrm{TT.after}(s)$ holds once $t - 2\varepsilon_{\max} > t_0 + 2\varepsilon_{\max}$.

(c) Let $a$ occur in process $j$ at time $t$ and $b$ in process $i \neq j$ with $a \to b$, so $b$ occurs at some $t_b \geq t + \mu$. Clocks are never set back, so
$C_i(t_b) \geq C_i(t + \mu)$, and by PC1, $C_i(t + \mu) - C_i(t) > (1 - \kappa)\mu \geq \varepsilon$. By PC2, $C_i(t) > C_j(t) - \varepsilon$. Adding,
$C_i(t_b) > C_j(t)$, that is $C(b) > C(a)$. $\square$

Part (a) needs no bound on clock error beyond TrueTime's guarantee; the error enters only the waiting time of part (b), which Spanner states as "the expected
wait is at least $2\varepsilon$" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.1]. Part (c) is Lamport's "easy to deduce" step [@lamport1978time, p. 563].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Part (a)'s proof on numbers. Each link of the chain is one rule.

::: {#exm-cw-chain}
#### The chain of inequalities

$T_1$'s request arrives at true time $100.000$ with interval $[99.996, 100.004]$, so $s_1 = 100.004$; its data become visible at $100.009$, when earliest is
$100.005$. $T_2$ starts at $100.010$, its request arrives at $100.011$ with interval $[100.008, 100.014]$, so $s_2 = 100.014 > s_1$.

```{.python .run}
s1 = 100.004; visible1 = 100.009; earliest_at_visible = 100.005
start2, arrive2, latest2 = 100.010, 100.011, 100.014
chain = [s1 < earliest_at_visible <= visible1, visible1 < start2 <= arrive2, arrive2 <= latest2]
print("links hold:", chain, "| s1 < s2:", s1 < latest2)
```

```{.text .run-output}
links hold: [True, True, True] | s1 < s2: True
```
:::

Part (a) in many random runs. Clocks have random errors within their intervals.

::: {#exm-cw-sim}
#### Commit wait in a simulation

Transactions arrive on servers whose intervals have random offsets inside them; with commit wait no pair violates item 4, without it some do.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(35)
def interval(t, eps=0.004):
    off = random.uniform(-eps, eps)            # the true time is somewhere in the interval
    return t + off - eps, t + off + eps
def run(wait):
    bad = 0
    for _ in range(20000):
        t1 = random.uniform(0, 1)
        s1 = interval(t1)[1]
        vis = t1
        if wait:
            while interval(vis)[0] <= s1: vis += 0.0005
        t2 = vis + random.uniform(0, 0.003)    # T2 starts after T1 is visible
        s2 = interval(t2)[1]
        bad += s2 <= s1
    return bad
print("violations without wait:", run(False), "| with wait:", run(True))
```

```{.text .run-output}
violations without wait: 6725 | with wait: 0
```
:::

Part (b) over Spanner's range of uncertainties. The wait is twice the uncertainty in the symmetric case.

::: {#exm-cw-wait-eps}
#### Commit wait against uncertainty

For $\varepsilon$ from $1$ to $7\,\mathrm{ms}$ the wait runs from $2$ to $14\,\mathrm{ms}$; at the average $4\,\mathrm{ms}$ it is $8\,\mathrm{ms}$, and Spanner measured "about $5\,\mathrm{ms}$"
[@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 5.1], less, because $\varepsilon$ is often below its average right after a poll and the measured runs were on one zone.

```{.python .run}
for eps in (1, 4, 7): print(eps, "ms ->", 2 * eps, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 ms -> 2 ms
4 ms -> 8 ms
7 ms -> 14 ms
```
:::

Part (c) relates clock skew to the fastest relation between events. Light sets a lower bound on it.

::: {#exm-cw-lamport}
#### Lamport's condition in numbers

Lamport notes that one "can always choose $\mu$ equal to the shortest distance between processes divided by the speed of light" [@lamport1978time, p. 563].
For servers $3000\,\mathrm{km}$ apart, $\mu = 10\,\mathrm{ms}$, so clocks with skew below $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ and negligible drift already satisfy the strong clock
condition for events related through any channel.

```{.python .run}
d, c = 3e6, 3e8
print(f"mu = {d / c * 1e3:.0f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
mu = 10 ms
```
:::

For the phone call, $\mu$ is human time. Part (c) is then easy to satisfy.

::: {#exm-cw-human}
#### A human in the loop

Telling a friend takes seconds, so $\mu \geq 1\,\mathrm{s}$, and clocks with $\varepsilon$ of milliseconds satisfy part (c) by a wide margin; the hard case is a
relation through a fast channel the system does not see, such as two programs talking directly.
:::

Part (d) estimates the skew a synchronisation protocol achieves. It grows with the diameter.

::: {#exm-cw-theorem}
#### Lamport's bound

With $d = 3$, $\kappa = 10^{-6}$, messages every $\tau = 30\,\mathrm{s}$ and unpredictable delay $\xi = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, $\varepsilon \approx 3(2 \times 10^{-6} \times 30 + 10^{-3})
= 3.2\,\mathrm{ms}$.

```{.python .run}
d, kappa, tau, xi = 3, 1e-6, 30, 1e-3
print(f"epsilon = {d * (2 * kappa * tau + xi) * 1e3:.2f} ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
epsilon = 3.18 ms
```
:::

A timestamp in the future can serve as a switch-over time. Spanner uses it for schema changes.

::: {#exm-cw-schema}
#### Atomic schema changes

A schema change is given a timestamp $t$ in the future; reads and writes "may proceed if their timestamps precede $t$, but they must block behind the
schema-change transaction if their timestamps are after $t$" [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.2.3]. Part (a) makes the switch the same at every server.
:::

A transaction waits, but its server does not. Others proceed during the wait.

::: {#exm-cw-throughput}
#### Waiting does not reduce throughput

During commit wait the transaction holds its locks, so transactions on the same rows wait too; others are unaffected. A row written $100$ times a second
loses $8\,\mathrm{ms}$ of each $10\,\mathrm{ms}$ slot to waiting, $80\%$, if the writes are serialised by locks.

```{.python .run}
rate, wait = 100, 0.008
print(f"fraction of time a hot row is held in commit wait: {rate * wait:.0%}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
fraction of time a hot row is held in commit wait: 80%
```
:::

Part (c) forbids setting clocks back. Lamport says why.

::: {#exm-cw-reverse}
#### Setting a clock back

"We assume that when a clock is reset, it is always set forward and never back. (Setting it back could cause C1 to be violated.)" [@lamport1978time, p. 563]:
a clock set back could give a later event a smaller time on one process.
:::

Commit wait is about distributed time. On one machine a counter suffices.

::: {#exm-cw-single}
#### A single machine

A single database assigns increasing commit numbers, and any transaction that starts after another commits gets a larger one: external consistency for
free. TrueTime is needed because Spanner's coordinators are many machines without a shared counter.
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the chain of part (a) exhaustively on a grid. Any interval containing the true time will do.

::: {#exr-cw-proof-check}
#### Part (a) for random intervals

On a grid of times and intervals, check that whenever $T_1$ becomes visible after $\mathrm{TT.after}(s_1)$ and $T_2$'s request arrives later, $s_2 > s_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

This is part (a)'s chain with arbitrary containing intervals; the enumeration finds no counterexample, as the proof says it cannot.

## Python

A grid search.

```{.python .run}
import itertools
ok = True
for t1, a1, b1, tv, ev, t2, a2 in itertools.product([1.0], [0.0, 0.5, 1.0], [0.0, 0.5, 1.0], [1.5, 2.5, 3.5], [0.0, 0.5, 1.0], [2.0, 3.0, 4.0], [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]):
    s1 = t1 + b1                       # latest at t1, with t1 in [t1 - a1, t1 + b1]
    if not (tv - ev > s1): continue    # commit wait not yet over at tv
    if t2 <= tv: continue
    s2 = t2 + a2
    ok &= s2 > s1
print("no counterexample:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
no counterexample: True
```
::::
:::

The second exercise reaches part (b)'s general bound. Skewed intervals make the wait longest.

::: {#exr-cw-asym}
#### The worst wait

Find intervals of half-width $\varepsilon_{\max}$ that make commit wait close to $4\varepsilon_{\max}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

At $t_0$ the interval is $[t_0, t_0 + 2\varepsilon_{\max}]$, so $s = t_0 + 2\varepsilon_{\max}$; later intervals are $[t - 2\varepsilon_{\max}, t]$, so earliest passes $s$
only after $t_0 + 4\varepsilon_{\max}$. Both contain the true time.

## Python

The wait in that case.

```{.python .run}
eps, t0 = 0.004, 0.0
s = t0 + 2 * eps
t = t0
while not (t - 2 * eps > s): t += 0.0001
print(f"wait {t - t0:.4f} s = {(t - t0) / eps:.1f} eps")
```

```{.text .run-output}
wait 0.0161 s = 4.0 eps
```
::::
:::

The third exercise checks part (c) numerically. Clocks drift and are skewed within the bounds.

::: {#exr-cw-lamport-proof}
#### Lamport's inequality

Simulate two clocks with drift below $\kappa = 0.01$ and skew below $\varepsilon = 0.05$, and events related with delay $\mu = \varepsilon/(1 - \kappa)$. Check that
$C(b) > C(a)$ in every case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

This is part (c) with equality in its hypothesis; the simulation draws clock rates and offsets within the bounds and finds no violation.

## Python

Random clocks.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(36)
kappa, eps = 0.01, 0.05
mu = eps / (1 - kappa)
ok, n = True, 0
for _ in range(200000):
    ri, rj = random.uniform(1 - kappa, 1 + kappa), random.uniform(1 - kappa, 1 + kappa)   # PC1
    oi, oj = random.uniform(-eps, eps), random.uniform(-eps, eps)
    t = random.uniform(0, 1)
    if abs((oi + ri * t) - (oj + rj * t)) >= eps: continue                               # PC2 at time t
    n += 1
    Ca, Cb = oj + rj * t, oi + ri * (t + mu)        # a on process j at t, b on process i at t + mu
    ok &= Cb > Ca
print("cases", n, "| C(b) > C(a) in all:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
cases 149463 | C(b) > C(a) in all: True
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise violates part (c)'s hypothesis. Two programs in one rack talk directly.

::: {#exr-cw-mu-small}
#### A fast hidden channel

Two servers in one rack have skew up to $1\,\mathrm{ms}$; a program on one sends a value to a program on the other over a direct socket in $50\,\mu\mathrm{s}$,
outside the database. Can the strong clock condition fail, and what restores it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Yes: $\mu = 50\,\mu\mathrm{s} < \varepsilon = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$, so the receiver's clock can be behind the sender's by more than the delay. Commit wait restores it
for transactions, since it waits out the uncertainty before the data can leave; or the programs can carry timestamps, Lamport's first remedy.

## Python

The margin.

```{.python .run}
eps, mu = 1e-3, 50e-6
print("condition eps/(1-kappa) <= mu:", eps <= mu)
```

```{.text .run-output}
condition eps/(1-kappa) <= mu: False
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise uses part (d)'s estimate. Skew grows linearly in the diameter.

::: {#exr-cw-diameter}
#### Larger networks, larger skew

With $\kappa = 10^{-6}$, $\tau = 10\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\xi = 0.5\,\mathrm{ms}$, find Lamport's $\varepsilon$ for diameters $1$, $3$ and $10$, and the poll interval that keeps $\varepsilon$
under $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $d = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$\varepsilon \approx d(2 \times 10^{-5} + 5 \times 10^{-4})$: $0.52$, $1.56$ and $5.2\,\mathrm{ms}$. For $d = 1$, $2\kappa\tau + \xi < 10^{-3}$ needs $\tau < 250\,\mathrm{s}$. Hierarchies
of time servers keep $d$ small, as TrueTime's masters and daemons do.

## Python

The estimates.

```{.python .run}
kappa, tau, xi = 1e-6, 10, 0.5e-3
```
