```{.python .run}
for d in (1, 3, 10): print(d, f"{d * (2 * kappa * tau + xi) * 1e3:.2f} ms")
print("tau for 1 ms at d=1:", round((1e-3 - xi) / (2 * kappa)), "s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 0.52 ms
3 1.56 ms
10 5.20 ms
tau for 1 ms at d=1: 250 s
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise bounds a hot row's write rate. Locks are held through the wait.

::: {#exr-cw-hot-row}
#### Hot rows and commit wait

Writes to one row are serialised by its lock, and each holds it for its Paxos round of $9\,\mathrm{ms}$ overlapped with a commit wait of $2\varepsilon$. Find the
row's largest write rate for $\varepsilon = 4$ and $7\,\mathrm{ms}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each write holds the lock for $\max(9, 2\varepsilon)$: $9\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $\varepsilon = 4$, $14\,\mathrm{ms}$ for $\varepsilon = 7$, so at most $111$ and $71$ writes a second.

## Python

The rates.

```{.python .run}
for eps in (4, 7):
    hold = max(9, 2 * eps)
    print(eps, f"ms: {1000 / hold:.0f} writes/s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
4 ms: 111 writes/s
7 ms: 71 writes/s
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise looks at a read at the current time. It may have to wait too.

::: {#exr-cw-read-wait}
#### Waiting to read

A read-only transaction takes $s_{\mathrm{read}} = \mathrm{TT.now}().\mathit{latest}$. Why must a replica wait before serving it, and for at most how long with uncertainty
$\varepsilon$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The replica must have applied every write with timestamp up to $s_{\mathrm{read}}$, including those still in commit wait; a write with $s \leq s_{\mathrm{read}}$
becomes visible within its own wait. Since $s_{\mathrm{read}}$ is at most $2\varepsilon$ ahead of the true time, waiting until $\mathrm{TT.after}(s_{\mathrm{read}})$, at
most $4\varepsilon$ by part (b), suffices; Spanner refines this with its safe time [@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 4.1.3].

## Python

The bound.

```{.python .run}
for eps in (1, 4, 7): print(eps, "ms: wait at most", 4 * eps, "ms")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1 ms: wait at most 4 ms
4 ms: wait at most 16 ms
7 ms: wait at most 28 ms
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise sets a clock back. Part (c) and the start rule both break.

::: {#exr-cw-clock-back}
#### Why not set back

A server's clock is set back by $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ after an NTP correction. Give a pair of local events whose timestamps are then reversed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An event at reading $100.003$ and, after the reset, a later event at reading $99.999$: the second gets the smaller time on the same process, breaking even the
ordinary clock condition, as Lamport warns (@exm-cw-reverse). Corrections must slew the clock, running it slower, instead.

## Python

The readings.

```{.python .run}
readings = [100.001, 100.003]
readings.append(100.003 + 0.001 - 0.005)       # one millisecond later, after setting back 5 ms
print([round(r, 3) for r in readings], "| monotone:", readings == sorted(readings))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[100.001, 100.003, 99.999] | monotone: False
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise combines time sources. An interval must contain both or reject one.

::: {#exr-cw-two-clocks}
#### Two masters disagree

Two time masters report intervals $[10.000, 10.004]$ and $[10.006, 10.008]$. Can both be correct? What does TrueTime's daemon do with such reports?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

No: the intervals are disjoint, so at most one contains the true time. The daemon "appl[ies] a variant of Marzullo's algorithm [27] to detect and reject liars"
[@corbett2012spanner, Sec. 3], keeping the largest set of mutually consistent intervals.

## Python

A consistency check.

```{.python .run}
a, b = (10.000, 10.004), (10.006, 10.008)
print("overlap:", max(a[0], b[0]) <= min(a[1], b[1]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
overlap: False
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise prices commit wait for the photo service. It adds a few milliseconds to every upload.

::: {#exr-cw-photo}
#### Commit wait for uploads

Uploads commit metadata through a Spanner-like store with $\varepsilon = 4\,\mathrm{ms}$, replication of $9\,\mathrm{ms}$ overlapped with the wait, and $694$ uploads
a second at the peak. What does commit wait add to an upload, and how many transactions are in commit wait at once?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It adds nothing to latency, since $2\varepsilon = 8 < 9$. By Little's law (@thm-littles-law), $694 \times 0.008 = 5.6$ transactions are in commit wait on average.

## Python

The numbers.

```{.python .run}
eps, paxos, lam = 0.004, 0.009, 3 * 2e7 / 86400
print("added latency", max(0, 2 * eps - paxos) * 1e3, "ms | in commit wait on average", round(lam * 2 * eps, 1))
```

```{.text .run-output}
added latency 0.0 ms | in commit wait on average 5.6
```
::::
:::

::::

## Sagas {#sec-sagas}

Where atomic commitment is too costly or impossible, a long change is split into local transactions that each commit at once, with a way back if a later
one fails. Tan: "A saga is a long-lived transaction that can be written as a sequence of transactions. All transactions must complete successfully, or
compensating transactions are run to roll back the executed transactions" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6, p. 115]. This section defines sagas,
compensations, and their coordination by choreography or orchestration, and proves what an aborted saga restores.

For more on this topic, see @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 5.5-5.6, pp. 114-120], @gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 8, "Employing the
Saga pattern"] and @gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024 [Ch. 10, pp. 314 and 326-329]. Gilbert notes that the pattern "was first discussed by Hector Garcia-Molina
and Kenneth Salem in their 1987 Princeton University paper entitled SAGAS" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Employing the Saga
pattern"]; that paper was not available for this chapter.

### Steps, compensations and coordination

A saga moves forward step by step and, on failure, backwards through compensations. @fig-sg-orchestration shows an orchestrated print order that fails at
the payment.

![An orchestrated saga for a print order: the slot is reserved, the payment fails, and the orchestrator releases the slot. Each arrow is a message through a
topic.](figures/saga_orchestration.svg){#fig-sg-orchestration width=75%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-saga}
#### Sagas, compensations and coordination

1. A **saga** is a sequence of local transactions $T_1, \dots, T_n$, each committed by one service, with **compensating transactions** $C_1, \dots, C_{n-1}$,
   where $C_i$ undoes the effect of $T_i$. If $T_k$ fails, the saga runs $C_{k-1}, \dots, C_1$; otherwise it commits $T_1, \dots, T_n$.
2. A step is **compensable** if it has a compensation, the **pivot** is the step after which the saga can no longer be undone, and the steps after the pivot are
   **retriable**: they are retried until they succeed.
3. In **choreography** each service reacts to the events of the others, and a service that cannot complete its step emits an **abort event** to which the
   others react with their compensations. In **orchestration** an **orchestrator** sends each step's command, receives its result, and decides the next step or
   the compensations.
4. A saga has no isolation: other transactions can see the effects of $T_1, \dots, T_{k-1}$ before the saga commits or compensates them.
:::

::::

Item 2 is Tan's: "Steps 1–4 are compensable transactions, which can be rolled back by compensating transactions. Step 5 is a pivot transaction. Transactions after
the pivot transaction can be retried until they succeed" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.1, p. 117]. Item 3 follows Tan's two sections and Gilbert:
"A boundary service emits an abort event when it is unable to complete its work" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Abort events"]. Item 4
is implied by Gilbert's remark that "multiple transactions may have interlaced and updated the same data since the previous transaction was executed"
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Compensating transactions"]; the sources read do not state it as a definition.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Tan's example books a flight and a hotel and then takes payment. Payment comes last for two reasons.

::: {#exm-sg-tour}
#### Tan's tour package

The payment service "should not process any payments until the airline ticket service confirms that the ticket is available, and the hotel room service
confirms that the room is available", and the user's payment details must stay with the company; "if a transaction to the payments service fails, the entire saga
should be rolled back in reverse order using compensating transactions on the other two services" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6, p. 115].
:::

The running example's saga has three steps. The payment is the pivot.

::: {#exm-sg-print}
#### The photo service's print order

$T_1$ reserves a slot at a print shop (compensation: release it), $T_2$ charges the card (pivot), $T_3$ sends the job to the printer and books shipping
(retriable). A failed charge releases the slot; once the charge succeeds, printing is retried until it succeeds.
:::

The print order over three `sqlite3` databases. The payment fails, and the slot is released.

::: {#exm-sg-sqlite}
#### A saga over three databases

Each service has its own database; the orchestrator runs the steps and, on the payment's failure, the compensation.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
shop, pay, ship = (sqlite3.connect(":memory:") for _ in range(3))
shop.execute("CREATE TABLE slots (slot INT PRIMARY KEY, order_id TEXT)"); shop.execute("INSERT INTO slots VALUES (1, NULL)")
pay.execute("CREATE TABLE charges (order_id TEXT, amount INT)")
ship.execute("CREATE TABLE jobs (order_id TEXT)")
def reserve(o):
    with shop: return shop.execute("UPDATE slots SET order_id = ? WHERE slot = 1 AND order_id IS NULL", (o,)).rowcount == 1
def release(o):
    with shop: shop.execute("UPDATE slots SET order_id = NULL WHERE order_id = ?", (o,))
def charge(o, card_ok):
    if not card_ok: return False
    with pay: pay.execute("INSERT INTO charges VALUES (?, 20)", (o,)); return True
def saga(o, card_ok):
    if not reserve(o): return "no slot"
    if not charge(o, card_ok): release(o); return "aborted, slot released"
    with ship: ship.execute("INSERT INTO jobs VALUES (?)", (o,))
    return "committed"
print(saga("o1", card_ok=False), shop.execute("SELECT * FROM slots").fetchall(), pay.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM charges").fetchone())
print(saga("o2", card_ok=True), shop.execute("SELECT * FROM slots").fetchall(), ship.execute("SELECT * FROM jobs").fetchall())
```

```{.text .run-output}
aborted, slot released [(1, None)] (0,)
committed [(1, 'o2')] [('o2',)]
```
:::

Gilbert insists that compensations add history. Nothing is erased.

::: {#exm-sg-gilbert-comp}
#### Compensation is not rollback

"A compensating transaction is not akin to a rollback. The objective is not to erase the evidence of the previous transaction. The previous transaction is a
historical fact, and the compensating transaction will become a fact as well ... mistakes are corrected by adding adjusting journal entries"
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Compensating transactions"]. A refund appears on the card statement next to the charge.
:::

In Tan's choreography the services talk through topics. The booking service only starts and ends it.

::: {#exm-sg-choreo}
#### A choreographed saga

The booking service produces a booking request; the ticket and hotel services consume it and produce payment requests; the payment service, having
"record[ed] the receipt of these events in a database", charges and produces a payment success event, which the others consume
[@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.1, pp. 116-117].
:::

Tan's orchestrator is a state machine. It holds only the sequence of steps.

::: {#exm-sg-orch}
#### An orchestrated saga

"An orchestrator is a finite-state machine that reacts to events and issues commands. The orchestrator must only contain the sequence of steps. It must not
contain any other business logic, except for the compensation mechanism" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.2, p. 117].

```{.python .run}
steps = ["reserve slot", "charge card", "send to printer"]
comp = {"reserve slot": "release slot"}
def orchestrate(results):
    done, log = [], []
    for step, ok in zip(steps, results):
        log.append(f"command: {step}")
        if not ok:
            log += [f"compensate: {comp[s]}" for s in reversed(done) if s in comp]; return log
        done.append(step)
    return log + ["saga committed"]
print(orchestrate([True, False, True]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
['command: reserve slot', 'command: charge card', 'compensate: release slot']
```
:::

Gandhi compares the two coordination styles. Each is good at what the other is bad at.

::: {#exm-sg-gandhi}
#### Trade-offs in Gandhi

Orchestration has a "centralized workflow" and consolidated "error handling", but is "slowed", "highly coupled", and the orchestrator "can become a bottleneck";
choreography has better "responsiveness and performance", "scalability" and "loose coupling", but error handling and state management are harder
[@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 10, pp. 327-329].
:::

Gilbert prefers orchestration once failures appear. The policy is in one place.

::: {#exm-sg-gilbert-orch}
#### Why compensations favour orchestration

"The choreography approach is reasonable for the happy path, but it begins to lose its appeal as the alternate paths begin to emerge"; "coordinating all the
compensations that are necessary in a long-lived transaction is best managed with orchestration because these policies are managed in one place"
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Abort events"].
:::

Gandhi gives the root of the problem. Each service commits alone.

::: {#exm-sg-gandhi-tx}
#### No commit across services

"When requests involve multiple microservices, you can't perform a single database commit or rollback for all updates. Since each microservice update is in its
own separate transaction, it must instead be committed or rolled back separately" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 10, p. 314]; Gandhi's remedy, if
consistency matters most, is to merge the services.
:::

Tan adds a periodic process that finishes or compensates stuck transactions. It is a safety net under sagas.

::: {#exm-sg-supervisor}
#### A transaction supervisor

"A transaction supervisor is a process that ensures a transaction is successfully completed or is compensated. It can be implemented as a periodic batch
job or serverless function"; Tan advises implementing it first "as an interface for manual review" since "automating compensating transactions is generally
risky" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.5, p. 114].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise reorders Tan's saga. Charging first makes the compensation a refund.

::: {#exr-sg-order}
#### Why the payment last

In the print order, compare charging the card first with reserving the slot first, when one order in ten finds no slot.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Charging first refunds one charge in ten, which users see and which costs fees; reserving first releases a slot, which nobody sees. Put the step most likely to
fail, and the cheapest to undo, first, and the hardest to undo last, as the pivot.

## Python

Compensations per $1000$ orders in each order.

```{.python .run}
n, p_no_slot = 1000, 0.1
print("charge first: refunds", int(n * p_no_slot), "| reserve first: slot releases 0, refunds 0")
```

```{.text .run-output}
charge first: refunds 100 | reserve first: slot releases 0, refunds 0
```
::::
:::

The second exercise classifies the steps of a saga. The pivot is the first step that cannot be undone.

::: {#exr-sg-pivot}
#### Finding the pivot

Classify the steps of an upload-to-print flow: reserve slot, charge card, print, ship, email receipt.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Reserve: compensable (release). Charge: compensable by refund in principle, but chosen as the pivot. Print: not undoable once paper is used, so it must come
after the pivot and be retriable. Ship and email: retriable. If printing can fail permanently, it should be the pivot instead, with the charge before it as a
compensable step.

## Python

The classification.

```{.python .run}
steps = [("reserve slot", "compensable"), ("charge card", "pivot"), ("print", "retriable"), ("ship", "retriable"), ("email receipt", "retriable")]
for s, k in steps: print(f"{s:14s} {k}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
reserve slot   compensable
charge card    pivot
print          retriable
ship           retriable
email receipt  retriable
```
::::
:::

The third exercise reads Tan's observation that choreographies may contain cycles. A cycle is not a loop of messages.

::: {#exr-sg-choreo-loop}
#### A cycle in choreography

Tan notes the cycle "hotel topic > payment service > payment topic > hotel service > hotel topic" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.1, p. 117]. Does it mean
messages circulate for ever?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

No: the hotel service produces a payment request once per booking, and reacts to the payment result by confirming, not by producing another request. The
graph of topics and services has a cycle, but each saga's messages follow a finite path through it, ended by the confirmation.

## Python

The messages of one booking.

```{.python .run}
path = ["hotel topic: payment request", "payment service", "payment topic: success", "hotel service: confirm (no new request)"]
print(" -> ".join(path))
```

```{.text .run-output}
hotel topic: payment request -> payment service -> payment topic: success -> hotel service: confirm (no new request)
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise checks Tan's comparison of message counts. It depends on the choreography.

::: {#exr-sg-double}
#### Twice the events?

Tan writes that in orchestration "the number of events is double that of choreography" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.3, p. 120]. Count the messages of a
linear saga of $n$ steps in both styles.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Orchestration: a command and a reply per step, $2n$. A linear choreography: each step's completion event triggers the next, $n$ events plus one final event to
the initiator, $n + 1$. So close to double for a chain; for Tan's parallel choreography, where services fan in at the payment service, the ratio differs.

## Python

Both counts.

```{.python .run}
for n in (3, 5, 10): print(n, "steps: orchestration", 2 * n, "| choreography", n + 1)
```

```{.text .run-output}
3 steps: orchestration 6 | choreography 4
5 steps: orchestration 10 | choreography 6
10 steps: orchestration 20 | choreography 11
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise compares latencies. Tan ties choreography to parallel requests and orchestration to linear ones.

::: {#exr-sg-latency}
#### Parallel and linear

The ticket and hotel steps take $120$ and $200\,\mathrm{ms}$, the payment $300\,\mathrm{ms}$, and each message $5\,\mathrm{ms}$. Find the latency of Tan's choreography,
with ticket and hotel in parallel, and of his linear orchestration. Is parallelism a property of choreography?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Choreography: $\max(120, 200) + 300$ plus three message hops, $515\,\mathrm{ms}$. Linear orchestration: $120 + 200 + 300$ plus six hops, $650\,\mathrm{ms}$. An orchestrator can
also send both commands at once and wait for both replies, $\max(120, 200) + 300 + 4 \times 5 = 520\,\mathrm{ms}$: parallelism is a choice of the saga, not of the
style.

## Python

The three latencies.

```{.python .run}
t, h, p, m = 120, 200, 300, 5
print("choreography", max(t, h) + p + 3 * m, "| linear orchestration", t + h + p + 6 * m, "| parallel orchestration", max(t, h) + p + 4 * m)
```

```{.text .run-output}
choreography 515 | linear orchestration 650 | parallel orchestration 520
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks Tan's claim that a saga has no state. Something must remember where it is.

::: {#exr-sg-stateless}
#### Does a saga have state?

Tan writes "A saga itself has no state" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6, p. 115], and also that an orchestrator "is a finite-state machine". Reconcile the two.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The saga's progress is state: which steps are done and which must be compensated. In orchestration it lives in the orchestrator, which must persist it to
survive a crash; in choreography it is spread over the services' records, such as the payment service recording which requests it has received. Tan's sentence
can only mean that there is no separate store for the saga as a whole.

## Python

An orchestrator that persists its state and resumes.

```{.python .run}
state = {"order": "o7", "done": ["reserve slot"]}     # persisted after each step
def resume(state, next_ok):
    return "continue with charge" if next_ok else "compensate: " + ", ".join(reversed(state["done"]))
print(resume(state, next_ok=False))
```

```{.text .run-output}
compensate: reserve slot
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise shows item 4. Another request sees a reservation that will be released.

::: {#exr-sg-dirty-read}
#### Reading a saga in progress

While the print order's payment is pending, another user asks for the shop's free slots and is told there are none. The payment then fails. What has the
second user seen, and how can the design soften it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An intermediate state, a slot that was never really taken: the saga's lack of isolation. A reservation can be marked as pending, as Tan's "AWAITING_PAYMENT"
state [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.1, p. 116], so that readers can treat it differently, for example by showing "possibly available".

## Python

The two views of the slot.

```{.python .run}
slot = {"status": "pending", "order": "o9"}
print("second user sees:", "free" if slot["status"] == "free" else "taken" if slot["status"] == "booked" else "possibly available")
```

```{.text .run-output}
second user sees: possibly available
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise makes a compensation fail. It must be retried until it succeeds.

::: {#exr-sg-comp-retry}
#### Compensations that fail

The release of a slot fails transiently with probability $0.2$. How many attempts does it take on average, and what must be true of the release for retries
to be safe?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Attempts are geometric with mean $1/0.8 = 1.25$ (@prp-retry-dlq (a) with no limit). The release must be idempotent: releasing a slot already released does
nothing, so a retry after a lost reply is harmless (@prp-idempotent-consumer).

## Python

A simulation.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(37)
att = []
for _ in range(100000):
    n = 1
    while random.random() < 0.2: n += 1
    att.append(n)
print("mean attempts", round(sum(att) / len(att), 3))
```

```{.text .run-output}
mean attempts 1.249
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise applies Gandhi's advice. Strong consistency between two services suggests one.

::: {#exr-sg-merge}
#### When to merge services

The photo metadata and the like counts are in two services, and the product requires that a deleted photo never shows likes. Would you build a saga, or merge
the services, by Gandhi's criterion?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Gandhi: "If data consistency and integrity are more important than any of the disintegrator forces, then it makes sense to combine the functionality into a single
microservice" [@gandhiHeadFirstSoftware2024, Ch. 10, p. 314]. Here a short window of stale likes is harmless, so a saga, or an event consumed by the likes service,
suffices; a requirement of no window at all would argue for merging.

## Python

The window with an event-driven delete, at a consumer lag of $2\,\mathrm{s}$.

```{.python .run}
print("likes visible after delete for up to about", 2, "s")
```

```{.text .run-output}
likes visible after delete for up to about 2 s
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise implements Tan's transaction supervisor. It finds sagas stuck between steps.

::: {#exr-sg-supervisor-scan}
#### A supervisor's scan

Sagas record their state with a timestamp. Write a scan that finds sagas pending for more than $10$ minutes and proposes the compensation, for review.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Select the sagas whose state is not final and whose last update is older than the threshold, and list the compensations of their completed steps in reverse
order; following Tan, an operator reviews them before they are run.

## Python

The scan over a table of sagas.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE sagas (id TEXT, state TEXT, updated INT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO sagas VALUES (?, ?, ?)", [("o1", "reserved", 0), ("o2", "committed", 0), ("o3", "reserved", 900)])
now = 1000
stuck = db.execute("SELECT id FROM sagas WHERE state NOT IN ('committed', 'compensated') AND ? - updated > 600", (now,)).fetchall()
print("propose release of slot for:", [s for (s,) in stuck])
```

```{.text .run-output}
propose release of slot for: ['o1']
```
::::
:::

::::

### What an aborted saga restores

A compensation undoes its step only if nothing else has happened in between, or if it is written to undo just its own change. The proposition makes both
precise, and the role of the pivot.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-saga}
#### Outcomes and compensations of a saga

Let a saga have steps $T_1, \dots, T_n$ and compensations $C_1, \dots, C_{n-1}$, each a local atomic transaction, let failed compensations and retriable steps
be retried until they succeed, and let the saga be coordinated as in @def-saga.

(a) Every run that ends has one of two outcomes: $T_1, \dots, T_n$ all committed; or, for some $k$, $T_1, \dots, T_{k-1}$ committed, $T_k$ failed, and
$C_{k-1}, \dots, C_1$ committed in this order.

(b) If no other transaction touches the saga's data and each compensation inverts its step on its service's state, $C_i(T_i(s)) = s$, an aborted saga leaves every
service in its initial state.

(c) Let the data be numbers changed by additions, let $T_i$ add $\delta_i$ and $C_i$ add $-\delta_i$, and let other transactions add amounts $\gamma_1, \gamma_2,
\dots$ at any times. Then an aborted saga leaves $x_0 + \sum_j\gamma_j$, whatever the interleaving; a compensation that instead restores the value read before
$T_i$ can erase other transactions' additions.

(d) If $T_1, \dots, T_{p-1}$ are compensable, $T_p$ is the pivot and $T_{p+1}, \dots, T_n$ are retriable, the saga commits if and only if $T_p$ commits, and no
compensation runs after $T_p$ has committed.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) The steps are tried in order. If all commit, the first outcome. Otherwise let $T_k$ be the first that fails; $T_1, \dots, T_{k-1}$ have committed, and
the saga runs $C_{k-1}, \dots, C_1$, each retried until it commits, so the run ends in the second outcome. Each step and compensation is atomic, so no service is
left with part of one.

(b) Service $i$'s state, for $i < k$, goes from $s$ to $T_i(s)$ and, since nothing else touches it, to $C_i(T_i(s)) = s$. Services $i \geq k$ have no committed
step: $T_k$ failed atomically and later steps never ran.

(c) Additions commute, so the final value is $x_0$ plus the sum of all additions made, in any order: $\delta_i$ and $-\delta_i$ for each compensated step, and
every $\gamma_j$. The $\delta$'s cancel. For the second claim: let $T_i$ read $x_0$ and set $x_0 + \delta_i$, let another transaction add $\gamma$, and let $C_i$
restore $x_0$; the result is $x_0$, and $\gamma$ is lost.

(d) If $T_p$ fails, $T_p$ is the first failure, and by (a) the saga compensates. If $T_p$ commits, the retriable steps after it are retried until they succeed, so
none is a first failure; by (a) all steps commit, and no compensation runs. $\square$

Part (c) is Gilbert's advice that when "multiple transactions may have interlaced and updated the same data", a compensation "may be as simple as subtracting the
incremental value instead of setting a discrete value" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Compensating transactions"]. Part (d) explains
Tan's pivot and retriable steps.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Part (a) by enumeration. Every pattern of failures gives one of the two outcomes.

::: {#exm-sgp-outcomes}
#### All outcomes of a three-step saga

For three steps, each succeeding or failing, the orchestrator's runs are enumerated.

```{.python .run}
import itertools
def run(results):
    done = []
    for i, ok in enumerate(results, 1):
        if not ok: return [f"T{j}" for j in done] + [f"T{i} failed"] + [f"C{j}" for j in reversed(done)]
        done.append(i)
    return [f"T{j}" for j in done]
for res in sorted(set(tuple(r) for r in itertools.product([True, False], repeat=3))):
    print(res, "->", run(res))
```

```{.text .run-output}
(False, False, False) -> ['T1 failed']
(False, False, True) -> ['T1 failed']
(False, True, False) -> ['T1 failed']
(False, True, True) -> ['T1 failed']
(True, False, False) -> ['T1', 'T2 failed', 'C1']
(True, False, True) -> ['T1', 'T2 failed', 'C1']
(True, True, False) -> ['T1', 'T2', 'T3 failed', 'C2', 'C1']
(True, True, True) -> ['T1', 'T2', 'T3']
```
:::

Part (b) for the slot reservation. Release inverts reserve when nobody else touches the slot.

::: {#exm-sgp-inverse}
#### Compensation in isolation

Reserve sets the slot's owner from none to the order, release sets it back: $C(T(s)) = s$.

```{.python .run}
reserve = lambda s: {**s, "owner": "o1"}
release = lambda s: {**s, "owner": None}
s0 = {"slot": 1, "owner": None}
print(release(reserve(s0)) == s0)
```

```{.text .run-output}
True
```
:::

Part (c) on the print shop's paper stock. Subtracting the increment keeps others' changes.

::: {#exm-sgp-additive}
#### Inventory with interleaving

A saga takes $10$ sheets; meanwhile a delivery adds $500$; the saga aborts. Adding $10$ back gives $1500$, the stock plus the delivery; restoring the old value $1000$
loses the delivery.

```{.python .run}
x0 = 1000
x = x0 - 10            # T: take 10
x += 500               # another transaction: delivery
additive = x + 10      # C: give back 10
restore = x0           # C: restore the value read before T
print("additive", additive, "| restore", restore, "| correct", x0 + 500)
```

```{.text .run-output}
additive 1500 | restore 1000 | correct 1500
```
:::

Part (d) for the print order. Once the charge succeeds, the order completes.

::: {#exm-sgp-pivot}
#### The charge as pivot

Printing fails transiently one time in five and is retried; every charged order is eventually printed, and no order is refunded after a successful charge.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(38)
printed = refunds = 0
for _ in range(1000):
    charged = random.random() > 0.05
    if not charged: continue          # compensate the slot; no refund needed
    while random.random() < 0.2: pass # retry printing
    printed += 1
print("printed", printed, "| refunds after a charge", refunds)
```

```{.text .run-output}
printed 944 | refunds after a charge 0
```
:::

Tan's orchestration has a pivot too. Steps after it cannot fail permanently.

::: {#exm-sgp-tan-retriable}
#### Retriable steps in Tan

"Steps 18 and 19 appear unnecessary, as step 18 will not fail; it can keep retrying until it succeeds" and "Steps 1–13 are compensable transactions. Step 14 is
the pivot transaction. Steps 15 onward are retriable transactions" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.6.2, p. 119].
:::

Part (c)'s additive compensation is accounting's adjusting entry. The ledger keeps both entries.

::: {#exm-sgp-ledger}
#### Compensation as a journal entry

A charge of $20$ and its refund are two entries summing to $0$; other entries in between are kept. This is Gilbert's analogy (@exm-sg-gilbert-comp), and the
ledger is event sourcing (@def-event-sourcing).

```{.python .run}
ledger = [("charge o1", -20), ("deposit", 100), ("refund o1", +20)]
print("balance change", sum(a for _, a in ledger), "| entries kept", len(ledger))
```

```{.text .run-output}
balance change 100 | entries kept 3
```
:::

A compensation is itself an event. Downstream services react to it.

::: {#exm-sgp-cascade}
#### Compensations have effects too

Gilbert: "It will also be necessary to account for the cascading effect of the events that will be produced by the compensating transaction. These events will
provide the audit trail, but they may also cause downstream services to react" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Compensating transactions"].
A released slot may trigger a notification to a waiting customer.
:::

An email cannot be unsent. It belongs after the pivot.

::: {#exm-sgp-email}
#### A step that cannot be compensated

An email receipt sent before the payment would need a "sorry, cancelled" email as its compensation, which part (b) cannot count as an inverse; placed after the
pivot it is retriable and never needs compensating, by part (d).
:::

Gilbert writes the orchestration of compensations as rules. Each abort maps to the cancellations it requires.

::: {#exm-sgp-gilbert-rules}
#### Compensation rules

The first rule "signals to the BFF W service to compensate when Step 1 or Step 2 aborts", the second "signals to the ESG X service to compensate when Step 2 aborts"
[@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 8, "Abort events"]: the reverse sequence of part (a), as a table.

```{.python .run}
rules = {"step1-aborted": ["request-cancelled"], "step2-aborted": ["step1-cancelled", "request-cancelled"]}
for abort, emits in rules.items(): print(abort, "->", emits)
```

```{.text .run-output}
step1-aborted -> ['request-cancelled']
step2-aborted -> ['step1-cancelled', 'request-cancelled']
```
:::

Item 4's window lasts as long as the saga. Little's law counts the sagas visible half-done.

::: {#exm-sgp-time}
#### How long a saga is open

Print orders arrive at $2$ per second and stay open $30\,\mathrm{s}$ until printed or compensated: on average $60$ are half-done at any time
(@thm-littles-law).

```{.python .run}
print(2 * 30)
```

```{.text .run-output}
60
```
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks part (a) for sagas up to six steps. Every run must end in one of the two outcomes.

::: {#exr-sgp-check-a}
#### Part (a) for every failure pattern

Enumerate all success patterns of sagas with $1$ to $6$ steps and check that the run is either all steps or a prefix followed by its compensations in reverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The proof of part (a) gives the run for the first failure $k$; the enumeration verifies the form for all $2^n$ patterns.

## Python

The enumeration.

```{.python .run}
import itertools
ok = True
for n in range(1, 7):
    for res in itertools.product([True, False], repeat=n):
        done, run = [], None
        for i, r in enumerate(res, 1):
            if not r: run = ("abort", done[:], list(reversed(done))); break
            done.append(i)
        if run is None: ok &= done == list(range(1, n + 1))
        else: ok &= run[1] == list(range(1, len(run[1]) + 1)) and run[2] == run[1][::-1]
print("all patterns have the two outcomes:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
all patterns have the two outcomes: True
```
::::
:::

The second exercise makes part (c)'s second claim concrete. Restoring a value is a lost update.

::: {#exr-sgp-lost-update}
#### A compensation that overwrites

A saga reserves one of $5$ free slots, setting the count to $4$; another order reserves one, setting it to $3$; the saga aborts and restores $5$. How many
slots does the shop think it has, and how many does it have?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It thinks $5$ and has $4$ free: the other order's reservation is lost, and a sixth booking can overbook. Adding $1$ back instead gives $4$, by part (c).

## Python

Both compensations.

```{.python .run}
free0 = 5
free = free0 - 1; free -= 1
print("restore:", free0, "| add back:", free + 1, "| true:", 4)
```

```{.text .run-output}
restore: 5 | add back: 4 | true: 4
```
::::
:::

The third exercise finds a compensation that cannot be an exact inverse. Fees make refunds lossy.

::: {#exr-sgp-not-inverse}
#### Compensations that are not inverses

A charge costs the shop a card fee of $0.30$ that the refund does not return. What does part (b) say about an aborted saga, and what does it cost?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$C(T(s)) \neq s$: the shop is $0.30$ poorer, so part (b) does not apply; only part (a)'s outcome holds. With one abort in ten among $10^4$ daily orders, $300$ a day;
a reason to place the charge as the pivot, after the steps most likely to fail.

## Python

The cost.

```{.python .run}
print(round(1e4 * 0.1 * 0.30, 2), "per day")
```

```{.text .run-output}
300.0 per day
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise breaks part (d)'s assumption. A retriable step must not fail permanently.

::: {#exr-sgp-retriable-fail}
#### A retriable step that fails for good

The printer is destroyed after the charge, so printing fails for ever. What does part (d) assume that no longer holds, and what must the design add?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

That retriable steps eventually succeed. Without it the saga never ends: the charged order waits for ever. A forward recovery outside the saga is needed, such as
routing the job to another printer, or an exceptional compensation (a refund) decided by an operator, Tan's transaction supervisor (@exm-sg-supervisor).

## Python

Retries capped to show the stuck saga.

```{.python .run}
attempts = 0
while attempts < 1000:
    attempts += 1          # printing fails every time
print("still not printed after", attempts, "attempts")
```

```{.text .run-output}
still not printed after 1000 attempts
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise asks why compensations run in reverse order. Later steps may depend on earlier ones.

::: {#exr-sgp-order-comp}
#### Compensating in reverse

Step $T_1$ creates an order row, $T_2$ adds a reservation referring to it. Why must $C_2$ run before $C_1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$C_1$ deletes the order row; if it ran first, the reservation would refer to a missing order, which a foreign key or a reader would reject. Reverse order undoes
dependent steps before the steps they depend on, as a stack.

## Python

Both orders.

```{.python .run}
def run(order):
    rows = {"order": True, "reservation": True}
    for c in order:
        if c == "C1":
            if rows["reservation"]: return "C1 fails: reservation still refers to the order"
            rows["order"] = False
        else: rows["reservation"] = False
    return "clean"
print("reverse:", run(["C2", "C1"]), "| forward:", run(["C1", "C2"]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
reverse: clean | forward: C1 fails: reservation still refers to the order
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise checks part (c) for random interleavings. Additive compensations always cancel.

::: {#exr-sgp-commute-check}
#### Part (c) by simulation

Simulate an aborted saga of three additive steps interleaved at random with ten other additions, and check the final value.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

By part (c) the result is $x_0 + \sum_j\gamma_j$ in every interleaving; the simulation shuffles the operations, keeping each $C_i$ after its $T_i$.

## Python

Random interleavings.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(39)
ok = True
for _ in range(2000):
    deltas = [random.randint(1, 9) for _ in range(3)]; gammas = [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(10)]
    ops = [("T", i) for i in range(3)] + [("C", i) for i in range(3)] + [("G", j) for j in range(10)]
    random.shuffle(ops)
    pos = {o: k for k, o in enumerate(ops)}
    if any(pos[("C", i)] < pos[("T", i)] for i in range(3)): continue
    x = 100
    for kind, i in ops: x += deltas[i] if kind == "T" else -deltas[i] if kind == "C" else gammas[i]
    ok &= x == 100 + sum(gammas)
print("final value is x0 + sum of others:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
final value is x0 + sum of others: True
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise softens item 4 with a flag. Readers can tell a pending change from a committed one.

::: {#exr-sgp-semantic-lock}
#### A pending flag

Show how marking reserved slots as pending until the pivot lets a second order treat them correctly, and what it may still do wrong.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A pending slot can be shown as "possibly available" and offered if the first saga aborts; booking it while pending would need its own compensation if the first
saga commits. The flag does not give isolation, it makes the lack of it visible, as Tan's "AWAITING_PAYMENT" state does.

## Python

Two orders and a pending slot.

```{.python .run}
slot = {"status": "pending", "by": "o1"}
second = "wait or offer another slot" if slot["status"] == "pending" else "book"
print("second order:", second)
slot["status"] = "free"                      # o1 aborted
print("after o1 aborts:", "book" if slot["status"] == "free" else second)
```

```{.text .run-output}
second order: wait or offer another slot
after o1 aborts: book
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise delivers a step's command twice. Steps must be idempotent too.

::: {#exr-sgp-duplicates}
#### Duplicate step messages

Commands travel through topics with at-least-once delivery. The charge command is delivered twice. What prevents a double charge, and what does part (a) then
need?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An idempotency key per order and step, recorded with the charge in one transaction (@prp-idempotent-consumer (b)); then each step's effect happens once, and
part (a), which assumes each step commits at most once, applies.

## Python

A charge with and without a key.

```{.python .run}
seen, charges = set(), 0
for msg in [("o1", "charge"), ("o1", "charge")]:
    if msg in seen: continue
    seen.add(msg); charges += 1
print("charges with key:", charges, "| without:", 2)
```

```{.text .run-output}
charges with key: 1 | without: 2
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise crashes the orchestrator between steps. Its persisted state lets it continue.

::: {#exr-sgp-orchestrator-crash}
#### An orchestrator that crashes

The orchestrator crashes after $T_1$ commits and before sending $T_2$'s command. Show that with its state persisted after each step, the run still ends in part (a)'s
outcomes, and what happens if it persisted nothing.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It recovers, reads "T1 done" and sends $T_2$; the run continues as if no crash happened, possibly repeating a command, which idempotent steps tolerate. With
nothing persisted, $T_1$'s reservation is orphaned: no step follows and no compensation runs, until a supervisor's scan (@exr-sg-supervisor-scan) finds it.

## Python

Recovery from the persisted state.

```{.python .run}
persisted = ["T1"]
def recover(persisted, steps=("T1", "T2", "T3")):
    return [s for s in steps if s not in persisted]
print("remaining after recovery:", recover(persisted), "| with nothing persisted:", recover([]), "(T1 would run again or be orphaned)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
remaining after recovery: ['T2', 'T3'] | with nothing persisted: ['T1', 'T2', 'T3'] (T1 would run again or be orphaned)
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise sizes item 4's exposure. Little's law counts the open sagas.

::: {#exr-sgp-open-count}
#### Half-done sagas at the peak

Print orders arrive at $5$ per second at the peak and a saga stays open for $40\,\mathrm{s}$ on average, of which $10\%$ abort and take another $20\,\mathrm{s}$ to compensate.
How many sagas are open on average?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Mean time open is $40 + 0.1 \times 20 = 42\,\mathrm{s}$, so $L = 5 \times 42 = 210$ by @thm-littles-law: $210$ orders are visible in an intermediate state.

## Python

The product.

```{.python .run}
lam, W = 5, 40 + 0.1 * 20
print(lam * W)
```

```{.text .run-output}
210.0
```
::::
:::

::::

## The transactional outbox, CDC and dual writes {#sec-outbox}

The messaging chapter introduced the transactional outbox in one sentence: the change and an outbox row are written "in one database transaction, and a relay
publishes the outbox rows and marks them as sent" (@def-event-sourcing, item 4, and @fig-es-outbox). This section makes the relay precise, adds
reconciliation for what a dual write loses, and proves what a relay publishes, in what order, and how long a reconciled difference can last.

For more on this topic, see @tanAcingSystemDesign2024 [Secs. 3.3.8, 5.3 and 5.5, pp. 63 and 112-114], @pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024
[Ch. 10, "Table diff", "Change Data Capture" and "Dual writing"], @gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024 [Ch. 5, "Database-first event sourcing"] and
@liuSystemDesignInterview2020 [Ch. 5, "Database and Queue"].

### Relays and reconciliation

The outbox turns two writes into one local transaction and a publication that can be repeated. What it cannot repair, reconciliation finds later.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-outbox}
#### Outbox relays, log tailing and reconciliation

1. An **outbox** is a table in a service's own database with one row per event to publish: an identifier, the payload and a mark that it has been sent. A change
   and the outbox row describing it are written in one local transaction.
2. A **polling relay** repeatedly selects the unsent outbox rows, publishes each to the broker, waits for the broker's acknowledgement and marks the row sent. A
   **log-tailing relay** reads the database's transaction log instead, and publishes each committed change.
3. A **dual write** (@def-event-sourcing, item 4) leaves the target missing changes when its second write fails. **Reconciliation** is a periodic process that
   compares a source with a target, by a **table diff** of their rows or by counts, and repairs the differences it finds.
:::

::::

Item 2's log tailing is Tan's "transaction log tailing pattern", where "a process called the transaction log miner tails a database's transaction log and produces
each update as an event" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.3, p. 113], and Pacheco's CDC, in which "you read the source database's log of all database changes,
and use that log to apply changes to a new target database" [@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 10, "Change Data Capture"]. Item 3's table diff is
Pacheco's: "you compare all the data in the source table with the data in a destination table, identifying the deltas" [@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024,
Ch. 10, "Table diff"]. The name "polling relay" is this chapter's.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The relay copies the outbox of one database into another, standing for the broker. Both are `sqlite3` files.

::: {#exm-ox-files}
#### An outbox relay over two database files

Three uploads commit with their outbox rows in `service.db`; the relay publishes them into `broker.db` and marks them sent.

```{.python .run}
import os, sqlite3
for f in ("service.db", "broker.db"):
    if os.path.exists(f): os.remove(f)
svc, brk = sqlite3.connect("service.db"), sqlite3.connect("broker.db")
svc.executescript("CREATE TABLE photos (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE outbox (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT, sent INT DEFAULT 0);")
brk.execute("CREATE TABLE topic (outbox_id INT, payload TEXT)")
for p in ("p1", "p2", "p3"):
    with svc:                                   # one local transaction
        svc.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES (?)", (p,))
        svc.execute("INSERT INTO outbox (payload) VALUES (?)", (f"uploaded {p}",))
def relay():
    for oid, payload in svc.execute("SELECT id, payload FROM outbox WHERE sent = 0 ORDER BY id").fetchall():
        with brk: brk.execute("INSERT INTO topic VALUES (?, ?)", (oid, payload))      # publish, acknowledged
        with svc: svc.execute("UPDATE outbox SET sent = 1 WHERE id = ?", (oid,))      # then mark
relay()
print(brk.execute("SELECT * FROM topic").fetchall(), svc.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM outbox WHERE sent = 0").fetchone())
```

```{.text .run-output}
[(1, 'uploaded p1'), (2, 'uploaded p2'), (3, 'uploaded p3')] (0,)
```
:::

An aborted transaction takes its outbox row with it. Nothing is published for it.

::: {#exm-ox-rollback}
#### A transaction that aborts

The second insert of a transaction violates a constraint, so the whole transaction rolls back, outbox row included.

```{.python .run}
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("CREATE TABLE photos (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY); CREATE TABLE outbox (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT);")
db.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES ('p1')"); db.commit()
try:
    with db:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO outbox (payload) VALUES ('uploaded p1 again')")
        db.execute("INSERT INTO photos VALUES ('p1')")       # duplicate key: the transaction aborts
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    pass
print("outbox rows:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM outbox").fetchone()[0])
```

```{.text .run-output}
outbox rows: 0
```
:::

Liu's first solution to the database-and-queue problem is the outbox's idea. The database does the enqueue in the same transaction.

::: {#exm-ox-liu}
#### Liu's database queue

"Some databases support a post-processing queue where the query to save the record and insert it into the queue is transactional. Sometimes this isn't an
option if the database doesn't come with queue support" [@liuSystemDesignInterview2020, Ch. 5, "Database and Queue"]. An outbox table makes any transactional
database such a queue.
:::

Tan lists tools that tail a database log. They are log-tailing relays.

::: {#exm-ox-tan-tailing}
#### Log miners

Debezium, Databus, DynamoDB Streams and Eventuate CDC Service "can be used as transaction log miners" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.3, p. 113]; they need no
outbox table, at the price of publishing row changes rather than chosen events (@exr-es-granularity).
:::

Pacheco uses dual writes on purpose, during data migrations. Their failure mode needs a remedy.

::: {#exm-ox-pacheco-dual}
#### Dual writes for migrations

In a dual write "teams write to two different databases at the same time"; among its drawbacks, "Failure: What happens if the write fails in one of the DBs? How
do you recover?", for which Pacheco's answer is to retry, or to "ignore it and let the table diff component take care of that"
[@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 10, "Dual writing"].
:::

Item 3 in code. A diff finds the rows the target lacks or has wrong.

::: {#exm-ox-diff}
#### A table diff

The source has four photos; the target missed one and has a stale caption for another.

```{.python .run}
source = {"p1": "sea", "p2": "cat", "p3": "dog", "p4": "sky"}
target = {"p1": "sea", "p2": "kitten", "p4": "sky"}
missing = sorted(set(source) - set(target))
wrong = sorted(k for k in source if k in target and source[k] != target[k])
target.update({k: source[k] for k in missing + wrong})
print("missing", missing, "| wrong", wrong, "| repaired:", target == source)
```

```{.text .run-output}
missing ['p3'] | wrong ['p2'] | repaired: True
```
:::

Table diffs read everything. Pacheco notes the limit.

::: {#exm-ox-pacheco-cost}
#### The cost of a diff

"Table diffs have limitations with large tables or datasets because you need to read the source table from time to time. You can reduce some of the impacts of
this technique by reading from a read replica instead" [@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 10, "Table diff"]. Diffing $10^9$ rows at $10^6$ rows a
second takes $17$ minutes.

```{.python .run}
print(f"{1e9 / 1e6 / 60:.0f} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
17 min
```
:::

Tan's periodic audit is reconciliation for writes that fail silently. It compares what was written with what was meant.

::: {#exm-ox-tan-audit}
#### Logging and auditing

"One method to handle silent errors is to log our write requests and perform periodic auditing. An auditing job can process the logs and verify that the data on
the service we write to matches the expected values" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 3.3.8, p. 63].
:::

Counts are a cheap diff. Kafka's pipeline audits itself this way.

::: {#exm-ox-kafka-counts}
#### Reconciling by counts

Each producer "periodically generates a monitoring event, which records the number of messages published by that producer for each topic within a fixed time
window"; consumers "count the number of messages that they have received from a given topic and validate those counts with the monitoring events"
[@kreps2011kafka, Sec. 4]. Counts detect a loss but not which message was lost.
:::

Gilbert publishes domain events from the database's own change stream. It is a log-tailing relay.

::: {#exm-ox-gilbert}
#### Publishing from the change stream

In database-first event sourcing a trigger function consumes the table's CDC stream and "produces a domain event to the event hub", relying "on the at-least-once
semantics of stream processing to help guarantee that we eventually publish the domain events" [@gilbertSoftwareArchitecturePatterns2024, Ch. 5,
"Database-first event sourcing"].
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise crashes the relay of @exm-ox-files between publish and mark. It republishes on restart.

::: {#exr-ox-relay-crash}
#### A relay that crashes

Crash the relay after publishing row $2$ and before marking it, restart it, and count the copies of each event in the broker.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Row $2$ is unsent on restart and is published again: two copies; the others one each. Consumers deduplicate by the outbox identifier
(@prp-idempotent-consumer (b)).

## Python

The crash and restart.

```{.python .run}
outbox = [{"id": i, "sent": False} for i in (1, 2, 3)]
topic = []
def relay(crash_after=None):
    for r in outbox:
        if r["sent"]: continue
        topic.append(r["id"])
        if r["id"] == crash_after: return
        r["sent"] = True
relay(crash_after=2); relay()
print({i: topic.count(i) for i in (1, 2, 3)})
```

```{.text .run-output}
{1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 1}
```
::::
:::

The second exercise reverses the relay's two steps. Duplicates become losses.

::: {#exr-ox-mark-first}
#### Marking before publishing

A relay marks a row sent and then publishes it. What does a crash between the two do?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The row is marked but never published, and the relay will not select it again: the event is lost. It is the acknowledgement-first order of
@prp-idempotent-consumer (a), at most once.

## Python

The crash.

```{.python .run}
outbox = [{"id": 1, "sent": False}]
topic = []
outbox[0]["sent"] = True       # mark
# crash before publishing
print("published:", topic, "| still selected later:", [r["id"] for r in outbox if not r["sent"]])
```

```{.text .run-output}
published: [] | still selected later: []
```
::::
:::

The third exercise sets the relay's polling interval. It adds to every event's delay.

::: {#exr-ox-polling}
#### How often to poll

The relay polls every $\Delta_p$ seconds. Find the mean and largest extra delay of an event, and the queries a day for $\Delta_p = 0.1$ and $1\,\mathrm{s}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

An event committed at a uniform time waits for the next poll: mean $\Delta_p/2$, at most $\Delta_p$. Polling costs $86400/\Delta_p$ queries a day: $8.6 \times 10^5$ and
$8.6 \times 10^4$. A log-tailing relay avoids the trade-off by being notified of new log entries.

## Python

Both intervals.

```{.python .run}
for dp in (0.1, 1.0): print(dp, "s: mean delay", dp / 2, "max", dp, "| queries/day", int(86400 / dp))
```

```{.text .run-output}
0.1 s: mean delay 0.05 max 0.1 | queries/day 864000
1.0 s: mean delay 0.5 max 1.0 | queries/day 86400
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise keeps the outbox small. Sent rows can go after a while.

::: {#exr-ox-cleanup}
#### Deleting sent rows

At $694$ events a second, how large is the outbox after a day if sent rows are never deleted, with $1\,\mathrm{kB}$ rows? When may a sent row be deleted?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$6.0 \times 10^7$ rows, $60\,\mathrm{GB}$ a day. A sent row may be deleted once the broker retains its event durably; keeping it for a few days helps reconciliation
and replay to the broker if the broker loses data.

## Python

The size.

```{.python .run}
rate = 3 * 2e7 / 86400
print(f"{rate * 86400:.2g} rows, {rate * 86400 * 1e3 / 1e9:.0f} GB per day")
```

```{.text .run-output}
6e+07 rows, 60 GB per day
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise simulates a dual write to a search index. One write in a thousand fails.

::: {#exr-ox-dual-loss}
#### What a dual write loses

Each upload writes the metadata store and then the search index, whose write fails with probability $10^{-3}$ and is not retried. Simulate $10^5$ uploads and
count the photos missing from search; then reconcile.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The run misses $119$, against $100$ expected, all found by a diff of identifiers and repaired, as item 3 says; between failure and repair, search silently lacks them.

## Python

The simulation and the repair.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(40)
store, index = set(), set()
for i in range(100000):
    store.add(i)
    if random.random() > 1e-3: index.add(i)
missing = store - index
index |= missing
print("missing before reconciliation:", len(missing), "| after:", len(store - index))
```

```{.text .run-output}
missing before reconciliation: 119 | after: 0
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise defeats a reconciliation by counts. A loss and a duplicate cancel.

::: {#exr-ox-counts}
#### Counts are not enough

A target has the same number of rows as the source, but one row is duplicated and another missing. Show that counts miss it and a diff by key finds it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Counts agree, $3 = 3$; a diff of the key sets finds the missing key and the duplicate. Counts are a cheap first check (@exm-ox-kafka-counts), not a proof of
equality.

## Python

Both checks.

```{.python .run}
source = ["p1", "p2", "p3"]
target = ["p1", "p1", "p3"]
print("counts equal:", len(source) == len(target), "| missing:", sorted(set(source) - set(target)),
      "| duplicated:", sorted({k for k in target if target.count(k) > 1}))
```

```{.text .run-output}
counts equal: True | missing: ['p2'] | duplicated: ['p1']
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise compares the two relays of item 2. They differ in what they publish and what they need.

::: {#exr-ox-tailing-vs-polling}
#### Log tailing or polling

List what each relay of item 2 needs from the database and what it publishes, and choose one for the upload events.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Polling needs only an outbox table and a query, and publishes the events the service chose to write. Log tailing needs access to the transaction log and a
tool to read it, and publishes every row change, with no extra table and no polling delay. For the upload events, whose payload the consumers rely on, the outbox
gives a stable contract (@exr-es-contract); log tailing suits copying tables to a search index.

## Python

The comparison as a table.

```{.python .run}
rows = [("needs", "an outbox table", "the transaction log and a reader"),
        ("publishes", "chosen events", "every row change"),
        ("delay", "polling interval", "log reading lag")]
for r in rows: print(f"{r[0]:10s} polling: {r[1]:18s} tailing: {r[2]}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
needs      polling: an outbox table    tailing: the transaction log and a reader
publishes  polling: chosen events      tailing: every row change
delay      polling: polling interval   tailing: log reading lag
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise makes Tan's transaction supervisor a reconciliation. It compares the saga's records with the services'.

::: {#exr-ox-supervisor}
#### Reconciliation for sagas

Tan's supervisor "periodically syncs the various destinations in case any writes fail" [@tanAcingSystemDesign2024, Sec. 5.5, p. 114]. For the print order of
@sec-sagas, what does it compare, and what does it do on a difference?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It compares charges with print jobs: a charged order without a job is a stuck saga, a job without a charge an error. It proposes the missing step or a
compensation, and, following Tan, logs every compensation and lets an operator approve it.

## Python

The comparison.

```{.python .run}
charges, jobs = {"o1", "o2", "o3"}, {"o1", "o3", "o4"}
print("charged without job:", sorted(charges - jobs), "| job without charge:", sorted(jobs - charges))
```

```{.text .run-output}
charged without job: ['o2'] | job without charge: ['o4']
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise reads Pacheco's first drawback. Only rows that are written get dual-written.

::: {#exr-ox-cold-data}
#### Dual writes miss cold data

During a migration by dual writes, $2\%$ of the $10^8$ photo rows are updated per day. What fraction has reached the new store after a week, and what completes it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Each row is untouched with probability $0.98^7 = 0.87$, so only $13\%$ has been copied: "dual writes only happen for data the service actively processes"
[@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 10, "Dual writing"]. A backfill driven by a table diff copies the rest.

## Python

The fraction.

```{.python .run}
print(f"copied after a week: {1 - 0.98 ** 7:.3f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
copied after a week: 0.132
```
::::
:::

The tenth exercise orders the outbox by identifier. Identifiers are assigned when rows are inserted.

::: {#exr-ox-order-insert}
#### Identifiers and commit order

Transactions $A$ and $B$ insert outbox rows $5$ and $6$; $B$ commits first. In what order does a polling relay publish them if it polls between the two commits, and
after both?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Between the commits it sees only row $6$ and publishes it; then row $5$: order $6, 5$, which is commit order. After both, it publishes $5, 6$, which is not. The
relay's order follows identifiers among the rows it sees, not commits.

## Python

Both polls.

```{.python .run}
committed_between = [6]
committed_after = [5, 6]
print("poll between:", committed_between, "then", [5], "| poll after both:", sorted(committed_after))
```

```{.text .run-output}
poll between: [6] then [5] | poll after both: [5, 6]
```
::::
:::

::::

### What a relay publishes

A relay publishes every committed change, possibly twice, and only those. How it remembers its progress decides whether it can skip one.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-outbox}
#### Guarantees of the outbox and of reconciliation

Let changes and their outbox rows be written in single local transactions, as in @def-outbox.

(a) If, from some time on, a polling relay runs without crashing and each publication is eventually acknowledged, every committed change is published at least
once; no change of an aborted transaction is ever published.

(b) A relay that marks a row after its publication is acknowledged publishes a row more than once only if it crashes, or loses the acknowledgement, between the
publication and the mark.

(c) A relay that remembers only the largest identifier it has published, and selects rows with larger identifiers, can skip a committed row for ever when
identifiers are assigned on insertion and transactions commit out of identifier order. A relay that selects rows by their unsent mark never skips one.

(d) If the second write of a dual write fails independently with probability $f$ and is not retried, the expected number of changes missing from the target after
$N$ writes is $fN$. If reconciliation starts at least every $P$ and repairs, within time $R$, every difference present when it starts, a change missing from the
target stays missing for at most $P + R$.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) A committed change's outbox row is committed with it, unmarked. From the time the relay stops crashing, each of its polls selects every unmarked
committed row; a selected row is published and, once acknowledged, marked. So every committed row is eventually published and acknowledged. An aborted transaction's
row was never committed, so no poll selects it.

(b) A row is published by a poll that selects it, which happens only while it is unmarked. After a publication is acknowledged and the row marked, no later poll
selects it. So a second publication requires a poll that selected the row after a publication but before the mark: a crash or a lost acknowledgement in between.

(c) Let row $5$ be inserted before row $6$ but committed after it, and let the relay poll between the two commits: it sees row $6$, publishes it and remembers $6$.
Every later poll selects identifiers above $6$, so row $5$ is never published. A relay selecting unmarked rows selects row $5$ at its next poll after the commit, as in
(a).

(d) Each of the $N$ second writes fails with probability $f$, so the expected number of failures, by linearity of expectation, is $fN$. A change missing from time
$t$ is still missing when the next reconciliation starts, at most $P$ later, unless repaired before; that reconciliation repairs it within $R$, so by $t + P + R$.
$\square$

Part (a) is why the outbox is the remedy of @exr-es-dual-write; part (c) is a failure that the "sent" mark of @def-event-sourcing avoids; part (d) prices Pacheco's
choice to "let the table diff component take care of" failed dual writes.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Part (a) with a broker that refuses one publication in ten. The relay keeps trying unmarked rows.

::: {#exm-oxp-retry-publish}
#### Publications that fail

A thousand committed rows are published by a relay whose publications fail with probability $0.1$; after enough polls all are published, some after several
tries.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(41)
unsent, polls, published = set(range(1000)), 0, set()
while unsent:
    polls += 1
    for r in sorted(unsent):
        if random.random() > 0.1: published.add(r); unsent.discard(r)
print("polls", polls, "| published", len(published))
```

```{.text .run-output}
polls 3 | published 1000
```
:::

Part (c)'s skip in a run. Two transactions commit out of identifier order.

::: {#exm-oxp-hwm}
#### Skipping with a high-water mark

Rows $5$ and $6$ commit in the order $6, 5$, with a poll in between; the high-water-mark relay never publishes $5$, the mark-based relay does.

```{.python .run}
committed = []
hwm, by_hwm, by_mark, sent = 0, [], [], set()
def poll():
    global hwm
    for r in sorted(committed):
        if r > hwm: by_hwm.append(r)
        if r not in sent: by_mark.append(r); sent.add(r)
    hwm = max([hwm] + committed)
committed.append(6); poll(); committed.append(5); poll(); poll()
print("high-water mark published", by_hwm, "| mark-based published", by_mark)
```

```{.text .run-output}
high-water mark published [6] | mark-based published [6, 5]
```
:::

Part (b)'s duplicates are harmless to a deduplicating consumer. The outbox identifier is the key.

::: {#exm-oxp-dedupe}
#### Duplicates at the consumer

A topic holds outbox events $1, 2, 2, 3$ after a relay crash; the feed consumer applies each identifier once.

```{.python .run}
topic = [1, 2, 2, 3]
seen, applied = set(), []
for oid in topic:
    if oid in seen: continue
    seen.add(oid); applied.append(oid)
print(applied)
```

```{.text .run-output}
[1, 2, 3]
```
:::

Part (d) for the search index. A thousandth of a day's uploads is twenty thousand photos.

::: {#exm-oxp-loss}
#### Expected losses of a dual write

With $f = 10^{-3}$ and $2 \times 10^7$ uploads a day, $2 \times 10^4$ photos a day are missing from search until reconciliation, against none with an outbox.

```{.python .run}
print(f"{1e-3 * 2e7:.0f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
20000
```
:::

Part (d)'s bound with an hourly diff. A photo can be missing for up to an hour and the diff's duration.

::: {#exm-oxp-window}
#### How long a photo is missing

With reconciliation every hour taking $10$ minutes, a missing photo is repaired within $70$ minutes; with a diff every $5$ minutes taking $1$, within $6$.

```{.python .run}
for P, R in ((60, 10), (5, 1)): print(f"P={P} min, R={R} min: missing at most {P + R} min")
```

```{.text .run-output}
P=60 min, R=10 min: missing at most 70 min
P=5 min, R=1 min: missing at most 6 min
```
:::

Part (a)'s second claim is what a dual write lacks. A dual write can publish an event and then fail to commit.

::: {#exm-oxp-abort}
#### Nothing from aborted transactions

Publishing first and committing second, a failed commit leaves an event for a change that never happened; the outbox cannot do this, since the event is a row
of the same transaction (@exm-ox-rollback).
:::

A relay that publishes rows one at a time in identifier order keeps that order in the topic. Commit order is a different matter.

::: {#exm-oxp-order}
#### Order of publication

Waiting for each acknowledgement before the next publication keeps the topic in the relay's order, as in @prp-consumer-group (b); by part (c)'s example, that
order follows identifiers, and two transactions that commit close together can appear in either order. Consumers that need order per entity rely on per-key
versions (@prp-idempotent-consumer (d)).
:::

A transaction log is written in commit order. A log-tailing relay publishes in that order.

::: {#exm-oxp-tailing}
#### Log tailing and commit order

Since the log records commits in the order they happen, part (c)'s skip and reordering cannot occur for a log-tailing relay that remembers its log position:
positions are assigned at commit, not at insert.
:::

Pacheco's alternative to the diff is to retry. Retries cap the loss but not to zero.

::: {#exm-oxp-pacheco-retry}
#### Retrying a dual write

Retrying a failed second write three times with independent failures of $10^{-3}$ leaves $10^{-12}$ of writes missing, but a crash of the writer between the two
writes still loses the second: Pacheco's "you also cannot retry forever, so after 3 attempts, what do you do?" [@pachecoPrinciplesSoftwareArchitecture2024, Ch. 10,
"Dual writing"].

```{.python .run}
print(f"{1e-3 ** 4:.0e}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
1e-12
```
:::

The relay of @exm-ox-files with failures. Every committed row reaches the broker database.

::: {#exm-oxp-two-files}
#### Part (a) across two files

Commits of $100$ uploads, a relay that crashes after random publications and restarts; the broker file ends with every row at least once.

```{.python .run}
import os, random, sqlite3
random.seed(42)
for f in ("svc2.db", "brk2.db"):
    if os.path.exists(f): os.remove(f)
svc, brk = sqlite3.connect("svc2.db"), sqlite3.connect("brk2.db")
svc.execute("CREATE TABLE outbox (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sent INT DEFAULT 0)"); brk.execute("CREATE TABLE topic (id INT)")
with svc: svc.executemany("INSERT INTO outbox (id) VALUES (?)", [(i,) for i in range(100)])
while True:
    rows = svc.execute("SELECT id FROM outbox WHERE sent = 0 ORDER BY id").fetchall()
    if not rows: break
    for (i,) in rows:
        with brk: brk.execute("INSERT INTO topic VALUES (?)", (i,))
        if random.random() < 0.05: break                      # crash before marking
        with svc: svc.execute("UPDATE outbox SET sent = 1 WHERE id = ?", (i,))
n, d = brk.execute("SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT id), COUNT(*) FROM topic").fetchone()
print("distinct published", n, "| total publications", d)
```

```{.text .run-output}
distinct published 100 | total publications 108
```
:::

::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks part (a) with random crashes and aborts. Every committed row and no aborted one must be published.

::: {#exr-oxp-proof-a}
#### Part (a) by machine

Simulate transactions that commit or abort at random, and a relay that crashes at random, and check part (a)'s two claims.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Proof

The proof's two arguments are the loop's invariants: committed unmarked rows are always selected, aborted rows never exist; the simulation confirms both.

## Python

The simulation.

```{.python .run}
import random
random.seed(43)
ok = True
for _ in range(500):
    committed = [i for i in range(50) if random.random() > 0.2]
    marked, published = set(), []
    while len(marked) < len(committed):
        for r in committed:
            if r in marked: continue
            published.append(r)
            if random.random() < 0.1: break            # crash before marking
            marked.add(r)
    ok &= set(published) == set(committed)
print("exactly the committed rows published:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
exactly the committed rows published: True
```
::::
:::

The second exercise repairs part (c)'s relay. It must not trust identifiers below the mark to be final.

::: {#exr-oxp-hwm-fix}
#### Fixing the high-water mark

Propose two ways to keep a high-water-mark relay while avoiding part (c)'s skip.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Assign identifiers at commit, as a log position is, so commit order and identifier order agree; or keep a safety margin, re-reading identifiers above the mark minus a
window and deduplicating, which works if no transaction stays open longer than the window. The unsent mark of part (c) needs neither assumption.

## Python

The window method on the example.

```{.python .run}
committed, published, hwm, window = [], set(), 0, 5
def poll():
    global hwm
    for r in sorted(committed):
        if r > hwm - window and r not in published: published.add(r)
    hwm = max([hwm] + committed)
committed.append(6); poll(); committed.append(5); poll()
print(sorted(published))
```

```{.text .run-output}
[5, 6]
```
::::
:::

The third exercise counts part (b)'s duplicates. They are as frequent as crashes in a short window.

::: {#exr-oxp-dup-rate}
#### How many duplicates

The relay crashes once a day, at a uniform time, and the window between publication and mark is $2\,\mathrm{ms}$ out of every $5\,\mathrm{ms}$ of work. How many
duplicates a day?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A crash falls in a window with probability $0.4$ and then duplicates one row: $0.4$ duplicates a day on average. Lost acknowledgements add more, one per lost
acknowledgement.

## Python

The fraction.

```{.python .run}
print("expected duplicates per day:", 2 / 5)
```

```{.text .run-output}
expected duplicates per day: 0.4
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise chooses $P$ from a freshness target. Part (d) gives the bound.

::: {#exr-oxp-diff-period}
#### Choosing the diff period

Search must not miss a photo for more than $15$ minutes, and a diff of recent rows takes $2$ minutes. What period $P$ is needed, and how many photos are missing at a
time on average with $f = 10^{-3}$ at $231$ uploads a second?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

$P + R \leq 15$ gives $P \leq 13$ minutes. A missing photo waits on average about $P/2 + R = 8.5$ minutes, so by Little's law about $231 \times 10^{-3} \times 510 = 118$
are missing at a time (@thm-littles-law).

## Python

The numbers.

```{.python .run}
P, R, lam, f = 13 * 60, 2 * 60, 2e7 / 86400, 1e-3
print("P =", P / 60, "min | missing at a time:", round(lam * f * (P / 2 + R)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
P = 13.0 min | missing at a time: 118
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise loses the broker's acknowledgement. The relay cannot tell it from a failed publication.

::: {#exr-oxp-ack-lost}
#### A lost acknowledgement

The broker stores an event and its acknowledgement is lost. What does the relay do, and which part of the proposition covers it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

It does not mark the row, so the next poll publishes it again: a duplicate, covered by part (b). Telling the two cases apart would need the broker to deduplicate by
outbox identifier, which moves the end-to-end check, but not the need for it, to the broker.

## Python

Publication with a lost acknowledgement.

```{.python .run}
topic, marked = [], False
for attempt in range(2):
    topic.append(7)                       # stored by the broker
    ack = attempt == 1                    # the first acknowledgement is lost
    if ack: marked = True; break
print("copies:", topic.count(7), "| marked:", marked)
```

```{.text .run-output}
copies: 2 | marked: True
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise asks what part (d)'s first claim needs. Linearity of expectation needs no independence.

::: {#exr-oxp-linearity}
#### Expected losses without independence

Show that $\mathbb E[\text{missing}] = fN$ holds even if failures are correlated, as in an outage, and what correlation does change.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Proof"}
